How can a waterjet cutter improve your machining speed and accuracy? Advantages of Waterjet Cutting Future Developments and Trends Conclusion How does CNC waterjet cutting operate and what does it entail? CNC waterjet cutting is a machining technique that uses a high-pressure stream of water combined with abrasive particles to accurately cut through diverse materials. The required shape or pattern is digitally modeled and then turned into a CNC program with the use of computer numerical control (CNC) technology. An intensifier, a cutting head assembly, and a high-pressure pump are all included with the CNC waterjet cutting machine. Although the cutting head assembly is moved by the CNC system, the water jet that is guided by the nozzle erodes the material. This technique is appropriate for a variety of applications because it offers great precision, low material waste, and the capacity to cut a broad range of materials. How can a waterjet cutter improve your machining speed and accuracy? In comparison to traditional machining procedures, a waterjet cutter improves machining speed and precision significantly. The fact that it cuts without making contact is one of its primary advantages. Since the cutting tool and the material are not in direct touch, there is no wear or damage to the tool, guaranteeing accurate and constant cutting performance throughout time. Waterjet cutters can attain high cutting speeds, particularly when abrasive particles are added to the waterjet stream. By efficiently eroding the material, the high-velocity waterjet facilitates faster cutting than with traditional machining techniques. Shorter production cycles and greater productivity are the results of this faster production. To further enhance precision multi-axis movement, waterjet cutters come with sophisticated CNC control systems installed. Due to its adaptability, precise and detailed cuts can be produced by using sophisticated and intricate cutting patterns. The CNC system accurately controlled the cutting head's movement, guaranteeing accurate results even with intricate geometries. The capacity of waterjet cutting to retain material characteristics and dimensional precision is an additional benefit. It doesn't produce heat during cutting because it's a cold-cutting procedure. This ensures that the finished product fulfills the required criteria by removing the possibility of thermal deformation or heat-affected zones in the material. In addition, the kerf width of waterjet cutters is relatively thin, usually between 0.1 and 0.3 millimeters. This narrow-cut size reduces material waste, enabling effective material utilization and lowering total production costs. Lastly, various materials, including metals, composites, stone, glass, polymers, and more, maybe cut through by waterjet cutters due to their extreme versatility. Because of its adaptability, waterjet cutting can be used in a wide range of sectors and industries, including the architectural, and creative industries. In summary, waterjet cutters are an effective tool for increasing machining speed and precision in several production processes because of their non-contact cutting, fast cutting speeds, precise multi-axis control, dimensional accuracy, tiny kerf width, and material diversity. Advantages of Waterjet Cutting With so many benefits, waterjet cutting is a popular cutting technique throughout an extensive variety of sectors. Its adaptability is one of its main benefits. Metals, stone, glass, polymers, composites, and many more materials may all be cut through with ease with waterjet cutting. The cold cutting technique of waterjet cutting is very beneficial since it produces no heat when cutting. Besides preventing material distortion, warping, or changes in material properties, this also prevents the creation of heat-affected zones (HAZ). Particularly useful for heat-sensitive materials are plastics and some metals. Another benefit is that the workpiece is subjected to very little mechanical stress during waterjet cutting. The non-contact cutting technique and the lack of mechanical forces reduce the possibility of material deformation or structural damage. Because of this, waterjet cutting is appropriate for materials that are brittle or sensitive and could be distorted or broken by other cutting techniques. Future Developments and Trends Waterjet cutting is set to undergo significant advancements and transformative trends in the coming years. Researchers and manufacturers are actively working towards increasing cutting speeds through technological innovations in pump systems, nozzle design, and abrasive delivery mechanisms. Precision and accuracy will be further enhanced by leveraging advancements in CNC control systems and motion control technologies, enabling intricate and complex cuts with tighter tolerances. Automation will play a larger role in waterjet cutting, with the integration of robotics for material loading and unloading, as well as seamless integration with other manufacturing processes to create efficient production lines. The utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning algorithms will optimize cutting parameters, predict tool wear, and improve overall cutting strategies. Multi-axis cutting capabilities will continue to advance, enabling waterjet systems to effortlessly navigate three-dimensional contours and shapes. Furthermore, the industry's focus on sustainability will drive efforts to minimize water consumption, reduce abrasive waste, and explore eco-friendly abrasive materials. Waterjet cutting will also find synergy with additive manufacturing processes, such as 3D printing, for post-processing tasks like support structure removal and precise finishing. These future developments and trends will shape waterjet cutting as an indispensable and versatile cutting method in various industries, offering increased speed, precision, automation, and environmental sustainability. Conclusion In conclusion, waterjet cutting offers numerous advantages in terms of machining speed and accuracy. Its non-contact cutting nature, high cutting speeds, multi-axis capabilities, minimal material distortion, narrow kerf width, and versatility with various materials make it a powerful tool for improving productivity and precision in manufacturing processes. Additionally, future developments and trends in waterjet cutting, such as increased cutting speeds, improved precision, enhanced automation, integration of AI and machine learning, eco-friendly solutions, and integration with additive manufacturing, promise even greater advancements and opportunities for the industry. As technology continues to evolve, waterjet cutting will remain a valuable and versatile cutting method for industries seeking efficient and accurate material processing. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals EDM Hole Drilling vs Conventional Drilling: Precision and Use Cases Compared Published Jul 24, 2025, updated Jul 18, 2025 5 min Table of Contents What Is Conventional CNC Hole Drilling? EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences When to Use EDM Hole Drilling When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? Limitations to Consider EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way Drilling a hole sounds simple, until you need to do it with extreme precision, into hardened materials, or to microscopic depths. That’s when you start comparing EDM hole drilling and conventional CNC drilling side by side. While both are designed to create holes, their technologies, capabilities, and ideal use cases couldn’t be more different. So, which method should you choose for your next project? Let’s dig in. What Is EDM Hole Drilling? EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining) hole drilling , also called hole popping EDM or EDM deep hole drilling , uses electrical sparks to erode material. Instead of a rotating drill bit, it uses a tubular electrode and dielectric fluid to remove metal through high-frequency discharges. It’s a non-contact process, meaning the tool doesn’t make direct physical contact with the material during machining. The result? It can drill extremely precise, burr-free holes even in hardened steel, carbides, or exotic alloys . What Is Conventional CNC Hole Drilling? CNC hole drilling uses rotating cutting tools<dynamic-value> twist drills or end mills, to cut into material. It's what most people imagine when they think about machining a hole. From high-speed spindles to peck drilling cycles, CNC machines are versatile and fast, especially when you're working with softer materials or mass production. But it’s still a contact-based process , and precision can degrade with wear, heat, or vibration. EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences Feature EDM Hole Drilling CNC Drilling Material Type Conductive materials only (e.g., steel, titanium) Any machinable material Tool Contact No physical contact Direct contact via tool Hole Size Micro to medium (0.1 mm to 6 mm) Wide range (0.5 mm to 50+ mm) Tolerance Extremely tight (±0.002 mm possible) Moderate (±0.05 mm typical) Hole Depth Excellent for deep, narrow holes (30:1+ depth-to-diameter) Limited by tool rigidity and chip evacuation Speed Slower Faster for larger holes Surface Finish Very smooth, no burrs May require deburring or finishing Tool Wear Minimal due to no mechanical contact High, especially in hard materials Are you unsure about which process is right for your metal part? We can help you choose the most precise and cost-effective method for your job. Get a free quote here and let's make your design manufacturable. When to Use EDM Hole Drilling The EDM hole drilling process shines in high-precision, small-diameter, deep-hole situations, especially where conventional drilling fails or causes tool breakage. Use cases include: ● Turbine blades (for cooling holes) ● Fuel injector nozzles ● Aerospace components ● Medical devices requiring micro holes ● Hard tool steels or materials like Inconel and titanium Also, EDM is ideal when you need starter holes for wire EDM , which conventional tools can’t drill due to hardness or geometry. When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling For general-purpose hole making in aluminum, plastics, or mild steel, CNC hole drilling is faster and more cost-effective. Use cases include: ● Bolt holes, pilot holes, tapped holes ● Large hole drilling in brackets or frames ● Machining production parts in batches ● Applications where tight tolerance is not critical And yes, to answer a common question, can a CNC machine drill holes? Absolutely. In fact, it’s one of the most common operations in any CNC shop. EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? EDM holes tend to be cleaner and burr-free straight off the machine. Their surface finish is smoother, with no mechanical stress or deformation around the hole. This makes them ideal for critical applications where dimensional stability and fatigue resistance matter. CNC-drilled holes, on the other hand, often need secondary processes , like deburring or reaming, to meet similar tolerances and finishes, especially in small diameters or deep holes. Limitations to Consider While EDM hole drilling offers unmatched precision, it’s not ideal for every scenario . ● It can’t be used on non-conductive materials (like plastic or glass). ● It’s relatively slow for large-diameter holes. ● Machines and electrodes are more expensive and require specialized operators. Conversely, CNC drilling tools wear faster in hardened materials, and the deeper you go, the higher the risk of tool deflection, chatter, or breakage . EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? A dedicated hole drilling EDM machine is typically compact, automated, and capable of producing holes as small as 0.1 mm in tough metals. Many come with automatic electrode changers and multi-axis positioning. For shops working with aerospace, mold making, or die sinking, having one on the floor is a game-changer for precision parts. Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way If you're prototyping intricate components or producing parts where one imperfect hole can ruin the entire build , go for EDM. But if you’re running production batches, drilling aluminum brackets, or cutting costs, CNC drilling is often more practical. Choose the Right Tool for the Hole Not every hole is created equal, and neither are the tools that make them. Whether you choose EDM hole drilling for ultra-precision or CNC hole drilling for speed and efficiency, understanding their strengths is the first step toward better manufacturing outcomes. If you’re unsure what your application calls for, talk to your machinist, or even better, partner with a shop that offers both options . Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals The Three Types of EDM Machining and How They Differ Published Jan 11, 2024, updated Aug 21, 2026 6 min Table of Contents What is and why do we use Electric Discharge Machining Materials and Applications in EDM Machining Differences between these three techniques Conclusion What is and why do we use Electric Discharge Machining EDM, or Electrical Discharge Machining, serves as a substitute for traditional machining methods when dealing with tough materials, particularly refractory metals and intricate shapes that are challenging to cut. Wire EDM enables the attainment of precision cuts with tolerances that would otherwise be unachievable, while hole drilling EDM excels in achieving precise diameters and roundness. Overall, EDM ensures exceptional precision and exceptionally low Ra levels, resulting in high-quality surface finishes. This characteristic reduces the need for extensive post-processing, ultimately lowering costs associated with manufacturing components that are notoriously difficult to produce. Technique 1: Hole Drilling EDM Hole Drilling EDM, also known as EDM Hole Drilling or EDM Micro-Drilling, is a specialized variant of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM). We specifically designed it to create precise and accurate holes in various materials, including metals and alloys. In Hole Drilling EDM, a small-diameter electrode, typically a rotating brass or copper tube, is used to generate a series of rapid electrical discharges. These discharges occur between the electrode and the workpiece, creating controlled erosion and gradually drilling a hole through the material. The process involves flushing a dielectric fluid, such as deionized water, through the electrode to flush away debris and cool the workpiece. The dielectric fluid also acts as a conductor for the electrical discharges. We value hole Drilling EDM for its ability to create highly accurate holes with tight tolerances, even in materials that are difficult to machine using conventional drilling methods. It is commonly used in industries such as aerospace, medical, automotive, and electronics, where precision holes are required for applications like cooling channels, fuel injection nozzles, or turbine blades. Technique 2: Sinker Discharge Machining Electrical discharge machining (EDM) is a type of procedure used for shaping and machining conductive materials. We refer it to as sinker discharge machining, sinker EDM, or conventional EDM. In Sinker Discharge Machining, a tool called a "sinker electrode" is used, which is typically made of graphite or copper. It shaped the sinker electrode to match the desired form or cavity that needs to be created in the workpiece. The process involves placing the sinker electrode close to the workpiece, with a dielectric fluid, such as oil or deionized water, acting as a medium between them. A series of electrical discharges, or sparks, are generated between the sinker electrode and the workpiece. These electrical discharges create controlled erosion, gradually removing material from the workpiece and shaping it according to the geometry of the sinker electrode. Sinker Release Intricate and complicated forms, such as molds, dies, and tooling components, are frequently made using machining. Because it does not need mechanical effort and doesn't create any noticeable heat-affected zones, it works especially well for cutting tough materials. Sinker EDM is capable of high accuracy and precise surface finishes, making it suited for sectors such as aerospace, automotive, tool and die manufacture, and medical device manufacturing. Technique 3: Wire Cut EDM Wire Cut EDM, also known as Wire Electrical Discharge Machining or Wire EDM, is a specialized kind of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) used for the precision cutting and shaping of conductive materials. A sequence of electrical discharges, or sparks, between the wire and the workpiece, are produced throughout the operation. The substance melts and evaporates because of the controlled erosion produced by these electrical discharges. The wire advances continuously, guaranteeing a continuous cutting action and enabling the machining of intricate forms and curves. Tight tolerances may be achieved, and wire-cut EDM is highly accurate. Cutting complex forms, thin sections, and contours in a variety of materials, such as metals, alloys, and conductive ceramics, is a popular use for it. Producing dies, molds, and tooling components for the precise engineering, automotive, aerospace, and electronics sectors is very helpful. Wire Cut EDM offers advantages, such as the ability to cut materials regardless of their hardness, minimal heat-affected zones, and the ability to achieve fine surface finishes. It is a flexible machining technique that allows for the high repeatability manufacturing of intricate and accurate components. Materials and Applications in EDM Machining EDM primarily handles materials that pose challenges for conventional machining methods, including tungsten, molybdenum, and hardened tool steels. Additionally, materials like titanium and austenitic stainless steels, which demonstrate significant work hardening during mechanical machining processes, are well-suited for EDM. As these materials harden while being machined, they become increasingly difficult to cut. Consequently, this hardening phenomenon often leads to a reduction in the accuracy of the machined part features. Electric discharge machining finds application in the production of molds for plastic injection molding and metal die casting. It is utilized to create intricate cavities in pre-hardened materials, showcasing its proficiency in achieving precise and complex cavity shapes, as well as executing deep cuts. Industries such as aerospace, automobile, and electronics also rely on EDM for fabricating prototypes and manufacturing various components. Differences between these three techniques Different types of EDM are classified based on their operations and applications. One example is wire EDM, which utilizes a linear feed wire electrode to make primarily two-dimensional cuts. We position the electrode wire on a guide made of diamond or sapphire, and the dielectric fluid used is typically deionized water. Brass or galvanized brass is commonly employed for the electrode material. In contrast, sinker discharge EDM allows for the utilization of intricate electrode shapes to create equally complex cavities. Graphite or copper electrodes are pre-machined into the desired shape and then eroded into the workpiece, resulting in holes that mirror the shape of the electrode. Drilling EDM is capable of producing smaller and deeper holes compared to traditional drilling methods. This enables precise diameters, roundness, excellent surface finishes, and eliminates burrs. Electrodes in drilling EDM can have intricate cross-sectional shapes. Drill tools often incorporate cooling channels through which dielectric fluid is circulated to aid in the removal of chips. Sinker discharge machining stands out as the most suitable type of EDM for fabricating components with intricate cavities. It enables the creation of complex cavity shapes frequently needed in the design of plastic and die-cast parts. While there are limitations to the range of cavity shapes achievable through sinker discharge EDM, these restrictions do not significantly affect its effectiveness as a tool for mold-making. The concept of the "line of the draw," which restricts EDM from producing undercuts, also applies to plastic molded and die-cast parts. These parts enter the tool cavity in liquid form but solidify as they exit. Conclusion To conclude, this article described the many forms of EDM machining, their differences, and when to utilize them. If you’ve ever needed a flat surface that’s actually flat , you’ve relied on it, whether you realized it or not. So what exactly is face milling? Think of it as the process behind every perfectly squared metal block, every smooth aluminum plate, every clean surface that just feels right. It’s precise, fast, and oddly satisfying to watch. But it’s not just about spinning a tool across some metal. The cutter design, tool path, speeds, and setup all play a role in getting that crisp finish without wrecking your inserts or your workpiece. In this guide, we’re breaking down how face milling works, what tools you’ll need, the types of operations involved, and a few tips that’ll save your cutters, and your sanity. What Is Face Milling? (istock) Face milling is one of the most common, and most essential, processes in the machining world. It’s all about cutting a flat surface perpendicular to the tool’s axis, usually with a wide face mill cutter that skims across the top of the material. The result? A smooth, level finish that’s ready for the next operation. Unlike side milling , which cuts along the edge or profile of a part, face milling focuses on creating a clean, wide face. It’s often the first step in squaring up a workpiece or prepping raw stock in a facing milling machine . What makes it effective is the tool design. A face mill tool typically uses multiple cutting edges (inserts) mounted in a circular holder. These inserts do most of the work, shaving off material in fast, controlled passes. You’ll find face mills in CNC shops, manual mills, and production floors alike, especially where consistency and finish quality matter. How the Face Milling Process Works The concept is simple: a rotating face mill sweeps across the surface of your material, cutting with the edges on the bottom of the tool. The setup, however, is where the real work begins. In a typical operation, the facing mill is mounted in a vertical spindle. As it spins, the inserts take shallow bites out of the material with each pass. The machine feeds the workpiece horizontally while the tool keeps cutting, layer by layer. It’s fast, consistent, and perfect for prepping a surface for tight-tolerance parts. The results depend on your setup, feed rate, cutting speed, tool path, and depth of cut all play a role. A roughing pass might take off more material quickly, while a finishing pass uses a finer face milling cutter for that clean, reflective finish. Tool rigidity and part stability matter. If your setup flexes, the finish suffers. If your inserts are dull, you’ll get chatter and uneven cuts. It's the kind of job where details make all the difference, and a decent face milling machine won't cover for poor planning. Roughing vs Finishing Parameter Roughing Finishing Depth of Cut 2–5 mm (0.08–0.2 in) 0.2–1 mm (0.01–0.04 in) Feed Rate Higher (aggressive) Lower (controlled) Cutting Speed Moderate Higher Tool Used Indexable face mill Fly cutter / fine-tooth mill Surface Finish Coarse Smooth (low Ra value) Common Face Milling Tools There’s more than one way to flatten a surface, and the tool you pick makes a big difference on your finish, your cycle time, and your tooling cost. Let’s break down the most common options used in face milling . Tool Selection Guide: When to Use What Tool Type Best For Pros Cons Face Mill Cutter General purpose, roughing + finishing Fast, efficient, easy insert swap Higher upfront cost Shell Mill Large parts, modular setups Versatile, scalable Needs arbor and holder setup Fly Cutter Finishing small to medium surfaces Inexpensive, smooth finish Slow, can vibrate at high speeds Solid Carbide Tool Light machines, tight spaces Rigid, compact Pricey, limited insert options Types of Face Milling Operations (ResearchGate) Face milling isn’t just about plowing a tool across a block of metal. There are different ways to run the cut, and knowing the options helps you get better results, or avoid screwing things up. Conventional Face Milling This is your go-to method. The face mill cuts across the entire top of the workpiece, removing material in overlapping passes. It’s efficient and ideal for prepping flat surfaces quickly. Partial Face Milling When the workpiece is smaller or has tricky geometry, only part of the face milling cutter engages with the material. It requires a bit more care in setup to avoid deflection and uneven cuts. Climb vs. Conventional Milling In climb milling, the cutter moves in the same direction as the feed, great finish, but it needs a solid machine. Conventional milling moves against the feed direction and offers more stability for older or lightweight machines. Some facing milling machines allow switching between the two. Slotting and Contour Facing Not every job is a square block. Face mills can be used for shallow slots or contoured faces if the toolpath is planned right. Just don’t expect perfect results unless your setup is rock solid. Face Milling Operations Summary Operation Type Description When to Use Conventional Face Milling Full-width surface passes General surface flattening Partial Face Milling Only part of cutter contacts surface Smaller or irregular workpieces Climb Milling Cutter feeds with the work Best for finish (requires stable setup) Conventional Milling Cutter moves against feed Safer on older or flexible machines Slotting / Contour Facing Shallow pockets or curved surfaces Non-flat geometries, careful setups Best Practices for Cleaner Face Milling ( reddit ) You can have the best tools on the shelf, but if you don’t dial in your technique, the finish will show it. Here’s what separates clean cuts from chewed-up messes. ● Keep your toolpath smooth—avoid sharp corners or direction changes mid-cut. ● Use coolant when possible. It extends insert life and keeps chips out of the way. ● Watch your depth of cut—too deep and you’ll get chatter, too shallow and the tool may rub instead of cut. ● Rigid setup matters more than fancy tooling. If your part moves, your surface finish suffers. And finally, picking the right tool geometry matters. The insert’s shape, rake, and edge prep can make or break your finish, especially on tricky materials. Tool Geometry Cheat Sheet: Choosing the Right Insert Material Recommended Geometry Rake Angle Notes Mild Steel Positive rake, round tip +10° to +20° Reduces cutting force, good surface finish Aluminum Sharp edge, polished +20° or more Prevents built-up edge, clean finish Stainless Steel Honed edge, tough grade 0° to +10° Needs stronger insert, avoid sharp corners Cast Iron Negative rake, strong edge 0° or negative Stable cut, handles interrupted surfaces Titanium Positive rake, low feed +10° Reduce heat, avoid rubbing Choosing the wrong insert isn't just a waste of money, it'll eat your surface finish alive Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling is one of those processes that rewards the prepared. The right face mill tool , a solid setup, and a bit of know-how can take your surface finish from “rough passable” to production-ready. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals The Advantages of Laser Cutting vs. CNC Milling for Sheet Metal Fabrication Published null, updated Mar 13, 2025 4 min In the field of sheet metal processing, laser cutting and CNC milling are two core processes known for their high precision, high efficiency and ability to process complex structures. Whether it's aerospace parts or consumer electronics housings, choosing the right processing technology has a direct impact on cost, efficiency and product quality. This article will be an in-depth comparison of laser cutting and CNC milling process advantages, analysis of its application scenarios, and provide companies with technology selection of the practical guide. I. Laser cutting: the perfect balance of speed and precision 1. Core process advantages Ultra-high precision: fibre laser cutting machine can achieve ±0.05mm tolerance (such as TruLaser 5030), smooth and burr-free cut. Wide material adaptability: support for stainless steel (0.5-30mm), aluminium alloy (0.5-25mm), copper plate (0.5-15mm) and so on. Processing efficiency: cutting speed up to 40m/min (1mm carbon steel), 3 times faster than traditional plasma cutting. 2. Typical application scenarios Thin plate precision processing: Electronic equipment shell (thickness 0.5-3mm), contour accuracy ≤ ± 0.1mm. Automotive sheet metal parts (such as door liners), cutting efficiency of 200 pieces / hour. Complex graphics processing: Artistic decorative metal screens, minimum hole diameter up to 0.2mm. 3. Cost-effectiveness analysis Case: a home appliance company processing 10,000 pieces of stainless steel panels: Laser cutting: single piece cost $ 8.5, time-consuming 3 days. Traditional stamping: mould cost $ 50,000 + single piece cost $ 6.2, the total cost is higher. II. CNC Milling: the ultimate solution for complex structures and high surface quality. 1. Core process advantages Three-dimensional machining capacity: five-axis CNC milling machine can process deep cavities, curved surfaces, shaped structures (such as impellers, mould cavities). Surface quality control: surface roughness Ra≤0.8μm after fine milling, directly achieve mirror effect. Batch consistency: Dimensional fluctuation of processing 1000 pieces of aluminium ≤ ± 0.02mm (CPK ≥ 1.67). 2. Typical application scenarios Thick plate precision parts: Aircraft engine bracket (50mm aluminium alloy), flatness ≤ 0.03mm. Hydraulic valve block (40CrMo steel), multi-hole system positional degree tolerance ± 0.01mm. Functional surface treatment: Mould insert nibble processing (VDI 3400 standard), texture depth 0.05-0.2mm. 3. Cost-effectiveness analysis Case: a medical device company processing titanium alloy joint implants: CNC milling: single piece cost $ 220, yield rate of 98%. 3D printing: single piece cost $ 380, need to follow up machining correction. III. Laser cutting vs CNC milling: four dimensions of comparison and selection guide Comparison Dimension Laser Cutting CNC Milling Applicable thickness Thin plate (0.5-25mm) Thick plate (5-300mm) Machining accuracy ±0.05mm (2D contour) ±0.01mm (3D structure) Material utilisation Nested nesting saves 15-30% of material. Clamping allowance needs to be reserved, lower utilisation rate Processing cycle Fast (no tool change, continuous cutting) Slow (multi-process tool change, suitable for complex parts) IV. How to choose the best machining process? 1. Selection decision tree Demand priority for ‘speed + cost’ → choose laser cutting. Demand priority is ‘complex structure + surface quality’ → choose CNC milling. Mixed demand: laser cutting + CNC milling finishing (20% lower overall cost). 2. What Is Laser Marking? Aluminum6061 laser marking Laser marking is a non-contact process that uses a focused laser beam to create visible or machine-readable identification directly on a manufactured part. The beam changes the surface condition rather than adding an external label or ink layer. Depending on the substrate and process settings, the mark may result from a surface-color change, oxidation, a change in texture, or localized coating or material removal. Common applications include serial numbers, part and revision codes, Data Matrix codes, and logos used for identification and traceability. The word "mark" covers several different surface changes. Which one you get depends on the material, the laser and the settings. Surface change What happens at the surface Where it typically shows up Oxidation (annealing) Heat forms a thin oxide layer that darkens or colors the surface Stainless steel, titanium Coating removal (ablation) The beam vaporizes a thin coating to expose the base metal Anodized aluminum, coated or painted metal Micro-recess or melted texture The surface melts or vaporizes slightly, changing roughness and reflectivity Bare metals Carbonization Heat chars or chemically darkens the surface Plastics, organic materials These surface-change mechanisms explain how laser marking can work across different substrates. They do not represent the complete list of materials or marking methods available for every JLCCNC order. Confirm material compatibility and the required appearance for the specific part. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote How Does the Laser Marking Process Work? Fiber laser marking system Preparing the Part and Marking File The marking artwork is loaded into the laser software in a supported format, with the part's marking face and position defined on the 2D drawing. The workpiece is positioned to maintain the required marking location and focus. Process settings are selected for the material and required surface effect, and a preliminary mark can be used to check contrast and detail before production. For new material and finish combinations, a sample mark can be used to confirm contrast and detail before production. Shops commonly run a test mark on a spare or scrap piece first. How the Laser Forms the Mark The laser system and its process settings must be suitable for the material and the required marking effect. In systems that use galvanometer scanning, mirrors steer the focused beam along the programmed path in the marking file. The focused beam concentrates energy in a localized area of the workpiece. Depending on the material and process settings, the interaction can change the surface color, modify the texture, remove a compatible coating, or remove substrate material to form a recess. The resulting mark depends on the interaction between the material, surface condition, and process settings. Verifying the Finished Mark Inspect the finished mark for edge definition, consistency of contrast, and conformity to the specified location. Check the marked area against the drawing requirements, including depth where specified. For machine-readable codes, verify readability using the intended scanner and inspection conditions. Verify machine-readable marks with the scanner and inspection setup used for the application. The laser etching guide linked above also recommends testing the code with the actual scanner you'll use in production. What Is the Difference Between Laser Marking, Laser Engraving, and Laser Etching? Term Typical surface change Material removal Result Laser marking Broad term for creating marks through laser-induced surface changes Depends on the method Visible identifiers, patterns, or codes Laser etching Usually creates contrast through a shallow surface modification Generally limited, depending on the process A visible mark with altered surface appearance Laser engraving Removes substrate material to create a recess Deliberate material removal A recessed mark that may be tactile These terms are not used consistently by every supplier, so the process name alone does not define the resulting feature. Specify the required appearance, recess depth where applicable, readability, and expected wear conditions. Suppliers do not always use these terms in the same way. In one quotation, "laser marking" may refer to a broad class of surface-modification processes; in another, it may describe a specific process. For reliable manufacturing results, define the required surface effect and measurable acceptance criteria instead of relying on terminology alone. Define the required appearance, recess depth where applicable, readability, and expected wear conditions. Specify whether the mark needs to contrast with the surrounding surface, whether a machine-readable code must pass a particular verification process, and whether later cleaning or surface treatments could affect the result. JLCCNC's design guide for laser marking specifies a recessed laser-marking depth of 0.03–0.1 mm. This is a JLCCNC-specific design specification, not a universal boundary between laser marking, etching, and engraving. Define the required appearance and depth on the drawing where applicable. Which Materials and Surface Finishes Can Be Laser Marked? How Material and Surface Finish Affect Marking Results The same artwork can produce different results depending on the material, surface finish and marking conditions. Reflectivity, roughness and existing coatings all affect contrast and final appearance. Material response and surface condition affect the resulting mark. Reflectivity, roughness, coatings, and the required surface effect all influence the process settings and the final contrast. Settings that work on one material or finish should not automatically be assumed to work on another. JLCCNC states that metal marking color is determined primarily by the characteristics of the material being marked, and its design guidance adds that results vary with surface roughness. A bead-blasted face and a smooth machined face won't look alike, even with identical settings. Surface treatments also affect the finished mark. Anodized aluminum and bare aluminum should not be assumed to produce the same contrast, even when the artwork is identical. Specify the actual surface finish and confirm the required appearance for that material before production. Materials Supported by JLCCNC JLCCNC offers laser marking for eligible CNC-machined and sheet metal parts. Material and finish availability depends on the selected manufacturing process and ordering requirements. Confirm the supported material, surface finish and marking requirements before production. Materials outside the confirmed laser-marking scope may require another identification method. UV printing is an alternative for compatible substrates when color is required, but material suitability should be confirmed before selecting the process. See JLCCNC's guide to laser marking vs. UV printing for a comparison of the two methods. Aluminum has its own behavior, especially anodized versus bare. Details live in our laser engraving aluminum article. Need laser marking for a custom part? Upload your CAD file for a project-specific quote. Define the marking surface and position on the 2D drawing, and provide the artwork in the required format. For sheet metal parts, follow the applicable file and ordering requirements. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote What Are the Benefits and Limitations of Laser Marking? Benefits of Laser Marking Technology Durability is a major advantage of laser marking. Because the mark is created by changing the surface rather than applying a separate adhesive label, it avoids label-edge peeling and ink-layer smearing. Long-term readability still depends on the marking method, material, surface finish, and service conditions. Laser marking does not require ink or adhesive label stock as part of the marking process, and the beam applies no stamping force to the workpiece. This avoids tool-to-part contact wear during marking, although the laser equipment and its optics still require appropriate maintenance. Laser marking can reproduce fine graphics and identification features without applying stamping force to the workpiece. Dot-peen marking creates physical indentations, while laser marking alters the surface through a laser-based process. The better option depends on the required appearance, readability, material, and operating environment. Machine-readable codes should be verified using the intended scanning setup. Laser marking is digitally controlled, so artwork can be revised without producing a new physical stamp or stencil. This can simplify mixed-batch production and product revisions, although actual cycle time depends on the graphic, the required surface effect, and the handling and verification steps involved. Limitations and Factors That Affect Marking Results These are the factors that decide whether a laser mark is the right call. Factor Why it matters What to specify Material and alloy Absorption and reflectivity change contrast Exact material and grade Surface finish and roughness Rough or uneven faces give inconsistent contrast Finish before marking Recess depth A shallow recess can wear through under heavy abrasion Wear and abrasion exposure Single-tone result Color follows the material, not the artwork Contrast expectations, not color names Geometry and access Curved or recessed faces change focus Which face, how flat Later finishing Blasting, plating or coating after marking can hurt legibility Mark after final finish where possible Any subsequent coating, blasting, heat treatment, or other finishing operation may alter the appearance or readability of a laser mark. Specify the complete process sequence and the required final appearance before production. What Are the Common Applications of Laser Marking? Part Identification and Traceability Laser marking supports part identification by placing a serial number, lot code, revision, or Data Matrix code directly on the component. When the identifier remains readable, production and inspection teams can link the physical part to its drawing revision, manufacturing records, and inspection results. Marking requirements vary by industry and application. Under U.S. FDA rules, a device that must bear a UDI on its label and is intended for repeated use and reprocessing generally must also carry a permanent direct marking, subject to applicable exceptions and alternatives. Automotive and aerospace manufacturers may also use serial numbers, part numbers, revision identifiers, or other traceability information according to their product and customer requirements. The marking method must be validated against the relevant requirements; laser marking alone does not establish regulatory compliance. On CNC-machined parts, the same practice applies at a smaller scale. A housing or bracket marked with its part number and revision allows incoming inspection to verify the part against the correct drawing revision. Logos, Labels, and Functional Markings Laser marking places a logo or product identifier directly on an enclosure or panel without requiring a separate adhesive label. Edge definition and contrast depend on the artwork, material, surface finish, and marking settings. The less obvious use is functional. Port and connector labels, orientation arrows, polarity marks, scale lines, calibration references, warning text on equipment panels. These aren't decoration. Incorrect or missing labels can create usability and safety issues on control panels. Laser-marked port labels, orientation arrows, polarity symbols, and warning text eliminate the need for a separate label, but readability should be checked against the expected cleaning and wear conditions. For special shapes, provide the exact marking location and a dimension frame with clear instructions. Marking Location and Positioning Dimensions Identify the marking face and dimension its location from defined datum edges. Avoid relying on a scaled image to communicate position. JLCCNC's design guidance recommends a marking margin of usually 3 mm to help prevent incomplete patterns. For special geometries, show the exact marking location and the required dimensions on the drawing. Artwork, Character Size, and Code Readability Keep the artwork geometry clean, with lines thick enough to preserve the intended detail after marking. JLCCNC's design guide recommends a design-file resolution of at least 300 dpi for clear, detailed results. For DWG or DXF artwork, supply clean geometry at 1:1 scale; for bitmap elements, ensure the source image has sufficient resolution. The guide does not specify a universal minimum character height, line width, or Data Matrix size for laser marking. For machine-readable codes, define the required reading result and verify the mark using the intended scanner under the relevant inspection conditions. Mark Depth, Contrast, and Surface-Finish Requirements JLCCNC's design guide specifies a recessed laser-marking depth of 0.03–0.1 mm. Define the required marking appearance and depth where applicable, and identify any expected abrasion or cleaning exposure. If the marked area lies near a critical feature, include its location on the drawing so the effect on the part's functional requirements can be reviewed. Laser marking produces a single-tone result determined by the material and surface treatment rather than a freely selected artwork color. Define the required contrast against the actual finished surface, and confirm the expected appearance for the specified material and finish. Keep the mark off threads, sealing faces and tight-tolerance features. The recess is shallow, but it's still a local surface change. And if the part gets anodized or coated, mark after the final finish unless the process requires otherwise. Laser Marking FAQs Q: Is Laser Marking Permanent? Yes, for normal service. The beam changes the surface itself, so the mark won't peel, smear or fade like ink or a label. "Permanent" has limits though. A shallow recess can wear through under heavy, repeated abrasion, and marks on anodized parts depend on the coating staying put. If the part will be sanded, blasted or re-finished later, say so before marking. Q: Does Laser Marking Affect Part Dimensions or Surface Finish? Laser marking can alter the local surface. Some methods mainly change color or texture, while JLCCNC’s published laser-marking guidance specifies a recessed depth of 0.03–0.1 mm for our service. Keep marks away from critical sealing, threaded, mating, and tight-tolerance features, and show their location on the drawing. Q: What Recessed Depth Does JLCCNC's Laser Marking Service Produce? JLCCNC's laser marking produces a recessed depth of 0.03 to 0.1 mm. That sits between typical laser etching and typical laser engraving figures, which is why it helps to specify appearance and wear needs instead of relying on the process name. Q: Can Laser Marking Be Applied After CNC Machining? Yes, and that's the normal sequence. Machine the part, finish it, then mark it. At JLCCNC you select laser marking under Surface Finish when you order CNC parts, so machining and marking happen in one workflow. Marking after the final finish keeps the mark from being altered by later steps. Q: What Affects the Cost of Laser Marking CNC Parts? Several things, though the quote tool gives the real number. Material and finish set the settings needed. Mark size and complexity drive machine time. Quantity spreads setup across more parts. And drawing quality matters more than people think: missing positioning dimensions or non-CAD artwork cause delays, and delays cost money. Laser Marking FAQs Key Takeaways Laser marking creates identification directly on a manufactured part by changing its surface condition with a focused laser beam. JLCCNC can produce a recessed marking depth of 0.03–0.1 mm for laser marking. The final appearance depends on the material and surface finish. A logo file shows what to mark, not where it belongs on the part. Dimension its position on the 2D drawing and supply DWG or DXF artwork at 1:1 scale. Bare aluminum and anodized aluminum can produce different results. A logo that looks black on screen will not necessarily appear black on the finished part. For detailed artwork, JLCCNC recommends providing design files with at least 300 dpi resolution. The design guide also recommends maintaining a 3 mm margin around the marking area to reduce the risk of incomplete patterns. A Data Matrix code needs to work with the production scanner, not just look readable to the naked eye. Aluminum enclosure with a laser-marked serial number Laser marking creates identification directly on a part rather than adding a separate ink layer or adhesive label. Depending on the material and marking method, it can be used for serial numbers, revision codes, logos, and machine-readable identifiers on metal housings, brackets, panels, and other manufactured components. JLCCNC provides laser marking as an available finishing option for eligible CNC-machined and sheet metal parts, allowing machining and marking requirements to be reviewed within the same project workflow. What Is Laser Marking? Aluminum6061 laser marking Laser marking is a non-contact process that uses a focused laser beam to create visible or machine-readable identification directly on a manufactured part. The beam changes the surface condition rather than adding an external label or ink layer. Depending on the substrate and process settings, the mark may result from a surface-color change, oxidation, a change in texture, or localized coating or material removal. Common applications include serial numbers, part and revision codes, Data Matrix codes, and logos used for identification and traceability. The word "mark" covers several different surface changes. Which one you get depends on the material, the laser and the settings. Surface change What happens at the surface Where it typically shows up Oxidation (annealing) Heat forms a thin oxide layer that darkens or colors the surface Stainless steel, titanium Coating removal (ablation) The beam vaporizes a thin coating to expose the base metal Anodized aluminum, coated or painted metal Micro-recess or melted texture The surface melts or vaporizes slightly, changing roughness and reflectivity Bare metals Carbonization Heat chars or chemically darkens the surface Plastics, organic materials These surface-change mechanisms explain how laser marking can work across different substrates. They do not represent the complete list of materials or marking methods available for every JLCCNC order. Confirm material compatibility and the required appearance for the specific part. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote How Does the Laser Marking Process Work? Fiber laser marking system Preparing the Part and Marking File The marking artwork is loaded into the laser software in a supported format, with the part's marking face and position defined on the 2D drawing. The workpiece is positioned to maintain the required marking location and focus. Process settings are selected for the material and required surface effect, and a preliminary mark can be used to check contrast and detail before production. For new material and finish combinations, a sample mark can be used to confirm contrast and detail before production. Shops commonly run a test mark on a spare or scrap piece first. How the Laser Forms the Mark The laser system and its process settings must be suitable for the material and the required marking effect. In systems that use galvanometer scanning, mirrors steer the focused beam along the programmed path in the marking file. The focused beam concentrates energy in a localized area of the workpiece. Depending on the material and process settings, the interaction can change the surface color, modify the texture, remove a compatible coating, or remove substrate material to form a recess. The resulting mark depends on the interaction between the material, surface condition, and process settings. Verifying the Finished Mark Inspect the finished mark for edge definition, consistency of contrast, and conformity to the specified location. Check the marked area against the drawing requirements, including depth where specified. For machine-readable codes, verify readability using the intended scanner and inspection conditions. Verify machine-readable marks with the scanner and inspection setup used for the application. The laser etching guide linked above also recommends testing the code with the actual scanner you'll use in production. What Is the Difference Between Laser Marking, Laser Engraving, and Laser Etching? Term Typical surface change Material removal Result Laser marking Broad term for creating marks through laser-induced surface changes Depends on the method Visible identifiers, patterns, or codes Laser etching Usually creates contrast through a shallow surface modification Generally limited, depending on the process A visible mark with altered surface appearance Laser engraving Removes substrate material to create a recess Deliberate material removal A recessed mark that may be tactile These terms are not used consistently by every supplier, so the process name alone does not define the resulting feature. Specify the required appearance, recess depth where applicable, readability, and expected wear conditions. Suppliers do not always use these terms in the same way. In one quotation, "laser marking" may refer to a broad class of surface-modification processes; in another, it may describe a specific process. For reliable manufacturing results, define the required surface effect and measurable acceptance criteria instead of relying on terminology alone. Define the required appearance, recess depth where applicable, readability, and expected wear conditions. Specify whether the mark needs to contrast with the surrounding surface, whether a machine-readable code must pass a particular verification process, and whether later cleaning or surface treatments could affect the result. JLCCNC's design guide for laser marking specifies a recessed laser-marking depth of 0.03–0.1 mm. This is a JLCCNC-specific design specification, not a universal boundary between laser marking, etching, and engraving. Define the required appearance and depth on the drawing where applicable. Which Materials and Surface Finishes Can Be Laser Marked? How Material and Surface Finish Affect Marking Results The same artwork can produce different results depending on the material, surface finish and marking conditions. Reflectivity, roughness and existing coatings all affect contrast and final appearance. Material response and surface condition affect the resulting mark. Reflectivity, roughness, coatings, and the required surface effect all influence the process settings and the final contrast. Settings that work on one material or finish should not automatically be assumed to work on another. JLCCNC states that metal marking color is determined primarily by the characteristics of the material being marked, and its design guidance adds that results vary with surface roughness. A bead-blasted face and a smooth machined face won't look alike, even with identical settings. Surface treatments also affect the finished mark. Anodized aluminum and bare aluminum should not be assumed to produce the same contrast, even when the artwork is identical. Specify the actual surface finish and confirm the required appearance for that material before production. Materials Supported by JLCCNC JLCCNC offers laser marking for eligible CNC-machined and sheet metal parts. Material and finish availability depends on the selected manufacturing process and ordering requirements. Confirm the supported material, surface finish and marking requirements before production. Materials outside the confirmed laser-marking scope may require another identification method. UV printing is an alternative for compatible substrates when color is required, but material suitability should be confirmed before selecting the process. See JLCCNC's guide to laser marking vs. UV printing for a comparison of the two methods. Aluminum has its own behavior, especially anodized versus bare. Details live in our laser engraving aluminum article. Need laser marking for a custom part? Upload your CAD file for a project-specific quote. Define the marking surface and position on the 2D drawing, and provide the artwork in the required format. For sheet metal parts, follow the applicable file and ordering requirements. Benefits of Laser Marking Technology Durability is a major advantage of laser marking. Because the mark is created by changing the surface rather than applying a separate adhesive label, it avoids label-edge peeling and ink-layer smearing. Long-term readability still depends on the marking method, material, surface finish, and service conditions. Laser marking does not require ink or adhesive label stock as part of the marking process, and the beam applies no stamping force to the workpiece. This avoids tool-to-part contact wear during marking, although the laser equipment and its optics still require appropriate maintenance. Laser marking can reproduce fine graphics and identification features without applying stamping force to the workpiece. Dot-peen marking creates physical indentations, while laser marking alters the surface through a laser-based process. The better option depends on the required appearance, readability, material, and operating environment. Machine-readable codes should be verified using the intended scanning setup. Laser marking is digitally controlled, so artwork can be revised without producing a new physical stamp or stencil. This can simplify mixed-batch production and product revisions, although actual cycle time depends on the graphic, the required surface effect, and the handling and verification steps involved. Limitations and Factors That Affect Marking Results These are the factors that decide whether a laser mark is the right call. Factor Why it matters What to specify Material and alloy Absorption and reflectivity change contrast Exact material and grade Surface finish and roughness Rough or uneven faces give inconsistent contrast Finish before marking Recess depth A shallow recess can wear through under heavy abrasion Wear and abrasion exposure Single-tone result Color follows the material, not the artwork Contrast expectations, not color names Geometry and access Curved or recessed faces change focus Which face, how flat Later finishing Blasting, plating or coating after marking can hurt legibility Mark after final finish where possible Any subsequent coating, blasting, heat treatment, or other finishing operation may alter the appearance or readability of a laser mark. Specify the complete process sequence and the required final appearance before production. If the part requires a pronounced tactile feature or must retain identification under severe abrasion, the appropriate marking method should be evaluated against those requirements rather than selected by name alone. What Are the Common Applications of Laser Marking? Part Identification and Traceability Laser marking supports part identification by placing a serial number, lot code, revision, or Data Matrix code directly on the component. When the identifier remains readable, production and inspection teams can link the physical part to its drawing revision, manufacturing records, and inspection results. Marking requirements vary by industry and application. Under U.S. FDA rules, a device that must bear a UDI on its label and is intended for repeated use and reprocessing generally must also carry a permanent direct marking, subject to applicable exceptions and alternatives. Automotive and aerospace manufacturers may also use serial numbers, part numbers, revision identifiers, or other traceability information according to their product and customer requirements. The marking method must be validated against the relevant requirements; laser marking alone does not establish regulatory compliance. On CNC-machined parts, the same practice applies at a smaller scale. A housing or bracket marked with its part number and revision allows incoming inspection to verify the part against the correct drawing revision. Logos, Labels, and Functional Markings Laser marking places a logo or product identifier directly on an enclosure or panel without requiring a separate adhesive label. Edge definition and contrast depend on the artwork, material, surface finish, and marking settings. The less obvious use is functional. Port and connector labels, orientation arrows, polarity marks, scale lines, calibration references, warning text on equipment panels. These aren't decoration. Incorrect or missing labels can create usability and safety issues on control panels. Laser-marked port labels, orientation arrows, polarity symbols, and warning text eliminate the need for a separate label, but readability should be checked against the expected cleaning and wear conditions. How Should CNC Parts Be Designed for Laser Marking? Define the marking face and positioning dimensions on the 2D drawing so the mark can be located without scaling an image. Supply the marking artwork in DWG or DXF at 1:1 scale, and clearly dimension the relevant geometry. JLCCNC recommends CAD-exported file formats and warns that machining precision cannot be guaranteed when other formats are used. For special shapes, provide the exact marking location and a dimension frame with clear instructions. Marking Location and Positioning Dimensions Identify the marking face and dimension its location from defined datum edges. Avoid relying on a scaled image to communicate position. JLCCNC's design guidance recommends a marking margin of usually 3 mm to help prevent incomplete patterns. For special geometries, show the exact marking location and the required dimensions on the drawing. Artwork, Character Size, and Code Readability Keep the artwork geometry clean, with lines thick enough to preserve the intended detail after marking. JLCCNC's design guide recommends a design-file resolution of at least 300 dpi for clear, detailed results. For DWG or DXF artwork, supply clean geometry at 1:1 scale; for bitmap elements, ensure the source image has sufficient resolution. The guide does not specify a universal minimum character height, line width, or Data Matrix size for laser marking. For machine-readable codes, define the required reading result and verify the mark using the intended scanner under the relevant inspection conditions. Mark Depth, Contrast, and Surface-Finish Requirements JLCCNC's design guide specifies a recessed laser-marking depth of 0.03–0.1 mm. Define the required marking appearance and depth where applicable, and identify any expected abrasion or cleaning exposure. If the marked area lies near a critical feature, include its location on the drawing so the effect on the part's functional requirements can be reviewed. Laser marking produces a single-tone result determined by the material and surface treatment rather than a freely selected artwork color. Define the required contrast against the actual finished surface, and confirm the expected appearance for the specified material and finish. Keep the mark off threads, sealing faces and tight-tolerance features. The recess is shallow, but it's still a local surface change. And if the part gets anodized or coated, mark after the final finish unless the process requires otherwise. Laser Marking FAQs Q: Is Laser Marking Permanent? Yes, for normal service. The beam changes the surface itself, so the mark won't peel, smear or fade like ink or a label. "Permanent" has limits though. A shallow recess can wear through under heavy, repeated abrasion, and marks on anodized parts depend on the coating staying put. If the part will be sanded, blasted or re-finished later, say so before marking. Q: Does Laser Marking Affect Part Dimensions or Surface Finish? Laser marking can alter the local surface. Some methods mainly change color or texture, while JLCCNC’s published laser-marking guidance specifies a recessed depth of 0.03–0.1 mm for our service. Keep marks away from critical sealing, threaded, mating, and tight-tolerance features, and show their location on the drawing. Q: What Recessed Depth Does JLCCNC's Laser Marking Service Produce? JLCCNC's laser marking produces a recessed depth of 0.03 to 0.1 mm. That sits between typical laser etching and typical laser engraving figures, which is why it helps to specify appearance and wear needs instead of relying on the process name. Q: Can Laser Marking Be Applied After CNC Machining? Yes, and that's the normal sequence. Machine the part, finish it, then mark it. At JLCCNC you select laser marking under Surface Finish when you order CNC parts, so machining and marking happen in one workflow. Marking after the final finish keeps the mark from being altered by later steps. Q: What Affects the Cost of Laser Marking CNC Parts? Several things, though the quote tool gives the real number. Material and finish set the settings needed. Mark size and complexity drive machine time. Quantity spreads setup across more parts. And drawing quality matters more than people think: missing positioning dimensions or non-CAD artwork cause delays, and delays cost money. Add laser marking in the instant quote to see pricing for your exact part. Types of Machining Burrs Why Machining Burrs Matter Burr Removal Methods Burr Removal Machines: Efficiency in Modern Shops Preventing Burrs in Machining Conclusion FAQs on CNC Machining Burrs CNC Machining Burrs (Envato) If you've ever run your hand across a freshly machined part and felt a sharp edge catch your skin, you've met the enemy: the burr. At first glance, it looks like a tiny flaw, but in machining, burrs are more than just a cosmetic annoyance. They can cut into assembly time, drive up costs, and in worst cases, create safety hazards for anyone handling the part. So, what is burr in machining? Think of it as the unwanted leftovers of the cutting process, those ragged edges, thin slivers, or raised ridges that show up after material is sheared, drilled, or milled. They're a headache for engineers and machinists alike because a part that isn't properly deburred can jam in an assembly, fail under stress, or even injure a technician. This is exactly why burr control matters so much in precision work. At JLCCNC, we've seen how burr-sensitive projects can make or break production runs, which is why we put the same focus on edge quality as we do on tolerances. And since our copper, steel, and aluminum machining starts at just $1 per part, even small shops can outsource tricky jobs and get parts that are both precise and safe to handle. What is Burr in Machining? (science direct) In machining, a burr is that unwanted bit of extra material left clinging to a part after a cutting process. Technically, it forms when the tool pushes or tears the material instead of slicing it away cleanly. What you get is a raised edge, a thin flap, or a tiny jagged lip that wasn't part of your CAD model, but now it's there, and it needs to be dealt with. You'll usually spot machining burrs around the usual suspects: along sharp edges, inside drilled holes, at the end of slots, or even wrapped around threads. Basically, anywhere the tool exits the cut is prime real estate for burr formation. Some are barely noticeable, while others can be sharp enough to slice a glove open or mess up an assembly fit. And here's the worst part: burrs aren't just a surface-level nuisance. They can ruin dimensional accuracy and surface quality, which is why deburring is almost always a required step in precision work. If you've read our guide on CNC Machining Surface Roughness: A Practical Guide , you'll know surface finish and edge quality often go hand in hand, burrs are just another part of that same equation. Types of Machining Burrs Not all burrs look the same, and knowing the type helps figure out the right removal method. Here's a quick breakdown of the most common machining burrs you'll run into: Burr Type Where It Shows Up What's Going On Poisson Burrs Along edges when cutting ductile metals Caused by plastic deformation pushing material sideways Roll-over Burrs Milling, drilling, and slotting operations Tool exit leaves a curled flap of material Breakout Burrs Exit side of drilled holes Material tears instead of shearing cleanly Cut-off Burrs Lathe parting or cut-off operations Extra material left behind as the tool separates the part Each of these has its own headache factor. A tiny Poisson burr might just ruin surface finish, while a chunky roll-over burr can jam an assembly or cut your hand open. Why Machining Burrs Matter (Intechopen) It's tempting to think burrs are just cosmetic, but they can cause problems way beyond looks. Here's why they matter: Impact Area How Burrs Affect It Assembly Tolerances Even a small burr can stop parts from fitting together cleanly Fatigue Life Burrs act as stress risers, shortening the lifespan of a component Safety Sharp burr edges can injure operators or end-users Post-Processing Costs Extra deburring steps = more time and money spent In high-stakes industries, one slip is all it takes. A single machining burr can cause part rejection in aerospace or medical applications, where safety margins are razor thin. And even outside of those fields, no customer wants a “finished” part that looks unfinished. Burr Removal Methods The method to remove burrs in CNC machining depends on part geometry, material, and how clean you need the finish. Here's a quick tour of the main approaches: Manual Deburring The old-school way: hand files, scrapers, sandpaper, or wire brushes. Cheap and flexible, but slow, and not consistent for production runs. Mechanical Methods Techniques like vibratory tumbling or grinding wheels are common in shops that need to batch-finish lots of smaller parts. Good for smoothing edges, but not always precise. Thermal Deburring Also called “explosive deburring.” Parts go in a sealed chamber, a gas mix is ignited, and burrs are literally burned off. Works well for internal burrs in tricky spots, but it's not the friendliest process for every material. Electrochemical Deburring This method uses an electrolyte and electric current to dissolve burrs in tight places<dynamic-value> cross-drilled holes or hydraulic components. Precise, but requires careful setup. Automated Deburring with Burr Machines This is where modern shops lean in. A burr machine uses abrasive brushes, rotary heads, or CNC-integrated tooling to remove burrs automatically. The result: faster turnaround, less operator fatigue, and a more consistent finish. Method Pros Cons Traditional (manual / mechanical) Low entry cost, flexible for odd parts Labor intensive, inconsistent, time-consuming Automated (burr machines) High speed, repeatable results, great for production Higher upfront cost, needs proper setup Burr Removal Machines: Efficiency in Modern Shops When people talk about shop efficiency today, burr machines and burr removal machines almost always come up. These systems combine abrasive heads, rotary tools, or even CNC attachments to take deburring from a bottleneck into a smooth step of the workflow. Machine Feature What It Does Why It Matters Abrasive Brushes Sweep away burrs on edges and surfaces Leaves a consistent finish without heavy labor Rotary Tools Target burrs in slots, grooves, or small features Great for complex part geometries CNC Integrated Deburring Toolpaths include deburring passes Saves setup time and reduces manual handling Benefits at a glance: faster cycle times, repeatable quality, and fewer operator hours spent hunched over a vise with a file. What is Burr in Machining? (science direct) In machining, a burr is that unwanted bit of extra material left clinging to a part after a cutting process. Technically, it forms when the tool pushes or tears the material instead of slicing it away cleanly. What you get is a raised edge, a thin flap, or a tiny jagged lip that wasn't part of your CAD model, but now it's there, and it needs to be dealt with. You'll usually spot machining burrs around the usual suspects: along sharp edges, inside drilled holes, at the end of slots, or even wrapped around threads. And here's the worst part: burrs aren't just a surface-level nuisance. They can ruin dimensional accuracy and surface quality, which is why deburring is almost always a required step in precision work.
