How to Reduce Waste in CNC Machining: 5 Practical Strategies Quick Answer: CNC machining waste is reduced mainly through DFM, near-net stock, efficient toolpaths, preventive tool maintenance, and alloy-segregated recycling. The biggest gains usually come before cutting: reduce unnecessary material removal and prevent scrap or rework. Every CNC-machined part starts as more material than it ends up being. A pocket gets milled out, a profile gets cut away, a boss gets faced down to size — and all of that removed material becomes waste, whether it's chips piling up in a bin or a block of expensive titanium reduced mostly to scrap. On some parts, the finished component is a small fraction of the raw stock's weight. Reducing that gap — without sacrificing the tolerances and finish a part actually needs — is less about any single trick and more about a handful of decisions made at different stages of the process, each with its own leverage. This guide covers the five main levers that actually move the needle on CNC machining waste, with links to deeper guides on the ones that have enough depth to warrant their own dedicated articles. Waste Types and Where They Come From Waste in CNC machining isn't one thing — treating it as a single category makes it hard to know what to fix first. It splits into four distinct types, each with a different cause and a different fix: Waste type What it is Mainly addressed by Unavoidable chips Material removed as part of normal subtractive machining — the literal byproduct of cutting a shape from solid stock Can't be eliminated, only recovered (Lever 5) Avoidable excess stock Material bought or left in the design beyond what the part actually needs — oversized billet, unnecessary wall thickness, stock faced away for no functional reason Levers 1 and 2 (design and material management) Scrap and rework Parts that fail to meet spec, or that require reworking, due to tolerance drift, poor finish, or tool-related defects Levers 3 and 4 (toolpath planning and tool maintenance) Spent tooling and coolant Worn cutting tools and used cutting fluid, treated as consumables but recoverable to a degree Lever 5 (recycling and reconditioning) Some of this is close to unavoidable — chips are the literal byproduct of subtractive machining — and some is genuinely reducible through better decisions upstream of the actual cutting. The five levers below map onto the "mainly addressed by" column above. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote How to Measure Waste Reduction Before comparing levers, it helps to have a way to tell whether any of this is actually working. Three metrics cover most of it: Material utilization rate = finished part weight ÷ raw stock weight. This is the clearest single number for how much of what you bought ended up in the part versus the chip bin. Scrap / rework rate = number of parts scrapped or reworked ÷ total parts produced. Tracks the second waste type in the table above — quality-driven waste rather than design-driven waste. Alloy-segregated recycling recovery rate = value or weight of chips recovered by alloy type ÷ total chip volume generated. Reflects how much of the unavoidable chip waste is actually being recovered rather than landfilled or sold as low-value mixed scrap. Tracking these turns "reduce waste" from a general goal into something a shop can actually measure improvement against. Lever 1: Design Optimization The cheapest waste to eliminate is the waste that never gets created in the first place, and design decisions made before a part ever reaches the machine have the biggest leverage on that. A part designed with excessive material where it isn't structurally needed gets machined down to size anyway — every bit of that unnecessary material becomes scrap. Reviewing a design specifically for material efficiency (not over-specifying wall thickness "to be safe," not adding stock that gets faced away for no functional reason) catches waste before it's ever cut. Our design for manufacturability guide covers this kind of review in more depth, including the broader set of DFM considerations beyond just material efficiency. Lever 2: Material Management How raw stock gets purchased, sized, and — where relevant — nested against a part's actual dimensions has a real effect on waste before machining even starts. Buying near-net-shape stock (raw material close to the finished part's dimensions) rather than machining a small part from an oversized block cuts waste dramatically on parts where that option exists. Nesting specifically applies to sheet or plate stock and multi-part jobs — arranging multiple part outlines efficiently across a sheet to minimize the material lost between parts. It isn't a general CNC billet concept; a single part machined from a solid block doesn't have a "nesting" decision to make the way a batch of flat-pattern parts cut from a sheet does. Material choice itself matters too, but the substitution logic has to run in the right order: the material still has to meet the part's performance requirements first. Only once a shortlist of materials clears that bar does it make sense to compare them on available billet sizes, how predictably each machines at the removal rates the job needs, and what the resulting chips are worth as segregated scrap. Swapping to a "more machinable" alloy that doesn't meet the part's actual requirements isn't a waste-reduction win. Lever 3: Strategic Machining (Toolpath and Process Planning) How the cutting itself is planned affects both direct material waste and the indirect waste from tool wear and rework. Efficient toolpath strategy — appropriate stepover, sensible roughing-to-finishing sequencing, avoiding unnecessary air-cutting or redundant passes — reduces both cycle time and the material removed less efficiently than it needs to be. Our guide on 5 CNC techniques to reduce waste in metal fabrication covers specific, actionable strategies at this level — smarter nesting, better blank sizing, intelligent toolpaths, optimized speeds, and simulation to catch problems before they become scrap. Lever 4: Tool Maintenance A dulling tool doesn't just cut less efficiently — it increases the risk of a part drifting out of tolerance or developing a poor surface finish, both of which can turn a nearly-finished part into scrap. Tracking tool wear against expected tool life, rather than running tools until they visibly fail, catches this before it produces bad parts. Our guide on tool wear detection and maintenance covers how to monitor this systematically rather than reactively. Lever 5: Waste Recycling What can't be avoided can often still be recovered. Metal chips have real scrap value and are commonly collected and recycled rather than landfilled — and for shops running enough volume, chip segregation by alloy meaningfully increases what that scrap is worth. Cutting fluid and coolant, often treated as a simple consumable, can be filtered, reconditioned, and reused rather than fully replaced on a fixed schedule. Our guide on zero-waste CNC strategies for recycling metal chips and coolant covers this specific piece of the waste picture — the recovery and recycling side, as distinct from the upstream prevention covered by the other four levers above. How to Prioritize These Five Levers Not every shop needs to tackle all five levers at once, and they aren't equally cheap to act on. A reasonable order to work through them: Check whether the billet or process itself can change first. Near-net-shape stock and process selection (Lever 2) are usually the single biggest lever available before any design or toolpath work happens. Then check whether the design is over-machining. A DFM review (Lever 1) catches unnecessary material and oversized stock allowances that would otherwise get machined away regardless of how efficient the toolpath is. Then reduce scrap and rework. Toolpath planning and tool maintenance (Levers 3 and 4) address the waste that comes from parts failing spec or requiring rework, which is often more expensive per part than raw material waste. Recover what's left. Recycling (Lever 5) is the last step because it deals with waste that's already unavoidable — chips and spent coolant that remain even after the first four levers are optimized. This order roughly matches how much control each lever has upstream of the actual cutting — the earlier a decision happens in this list, the more waste it prevents rather than merely recovers. What Not to Compromise When Reducing CNC Waste Treating waste reduction as purely a sustainability or compliance concern, separate from cost, undersells how directly it affects the bottom line. Every gram of scrap material is raw material that was purchased and then paid for again in machine time to remove — waste reduction is a cost optimization lever as much as an environmental one, and in most shops, the cost argument is what actually drives adoption. That said, waste reduction has a real failure mode worth naming directly: don't loosen functional tolerances, skip a necessary finishing pass, or lower a genuine quality requirement in the name of cutting material or cycle time. A part that comes back out of tolerance or fails in service because a step was cut to save material isn't a waste-reduction win — it's scrap with extra steps, and it usually costs more than the material it was meant to save. The "over-correcting" version of this mistake — tightening tolerances or adding excessive finishing passes in the name of "getting it right the first time" — is its mirror image, and can increase machining time and tool wear enough to offset whatever material savings were gained. Waste reduction works best as a set of deliberate, evaluated decisions at each of the five levers above — not a blanket instinct to cut corners, in either direction, everywhere at once. How to Reduce Waste in CNC Machining: 5 Practical Strategies Quick Answer: CNC machining waste is reduced mainly through DFM, near-net stock, efficient toolpaths, preventive tool maintenance, and alloy-segregated recycling. The biggest gains usually come before cutting: reduce unnecessary material removal and prevent scrap or rework. Every CNC-machined part starts as more material than it ends up being. A pocket gets milled out, a profile gets cut away, a boss gets faced down to size — and all of that removed material becomes waste, whether it's chips piling up in a bin or a block of expensive titanium reduced mostly to scrap. On some parts, the finished component is a small fraction of the raw stock's weight. Reducing that gap — without sacrificing the tolerances and finish a part actually needs — is less about any single trick and more about a handful of decisions made at different stages of the process, each with its own leverage. This guide covers the five main levers that actually move the needle on CNC machining waste, with links to deeper guides on the ones that have enough depth to warrant their own dedicated articles. Waste Types and Where They Come From Waste in CNC machining isn't one thing — treating it as a single category makes it hard to know what to fix first. It splits into four distinct types, each with a different cause and a different fix: Waste type What it is Mainly addressed by Unavoidable chips Material removed as part of normal subtractive machining — the literal byproduct of cutting a shape from solid stock Can't be eliminated, only recovered (Lever 5) Avoidable excess stock Material bought or left in the design beyond what the part actually needs — oversized billet, unnecessary wall thickness, stock faced away for no functional reason Levers 1 and 2 (design and material management) Scrap and rework Parts that fail to meet spec, or that require reworking, due to tolerance drift, poor finish, or tool-related defects Levers 3 and 4 (toolpath planning and tool maintenance) Spent tooling and coolant Worn cutting tools and used cutting fluid, treated as consumables but recoverable to a degree Lever 5 (recycling and reconditioning) Some of this is close to unavoidable — chips are the literal byproduct of subtractive machining — and some is genuinely reducible through better decisions upstream of the actual cutting. The five levers below map onto the "mainly addressed by" column above. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote How to Measure Waste Reduction Before comparing levers, it helps to have a way to tell whether any of this is actually working. Three metrics cover most of it: Material utilization rate = finished part weight ÷ raw stock weight. This is the clearest single number for how much of what you bought ended up in the part versus the chip bin. Scrap / rework rate = number of parts scrapped or reworked ÷ total parts produced. Tracks the second waste type in the table above — quality-driven waste rather than design-driven waste. Alloy-segregated recycling recovery rate = value or weight of chips recovered by alloy type ÷ total chip volume generated. Reflects how much of the unavoidable chip waste is actually being recovered rather than landfilled or sold as low-value mixed scrap. Tracking these turns "reduce waste" from a general goal into something a shop can actually measure improvement against. Lever 1: Design Optimization The cheapest waste to eliminate is the waste that never gets created in the first place, and design decisions made before a part ever reaches the machine have the biggest leverage on that. A part designed with excessive material where it isn't structurally needed gets machined down to size anyway — every bit of that unnecessary material becomes scrap. Reviewing a design specifically for material efficiency (not over-specifying wall thickness "to be safe," not adding stock that gets faced away for no functional reason) catches waste before it's ever cut. Our design for manufacturability guide covers this kind of review in more depth, including the broader set of DFM considerations beyond just material efficiency. Lever 2: Material Management How raw stock gets purchased, sized, and — where relevant — nested against a part's actual dimensions has a real effect on waste before machining even starts. Buying near-net-shape stock (raw material close to the finished part's dimensions) rather than machining a small part from an oversized block cuts waste dramatically on parts where that option exists. Nesting specifically applies to sheet or plate stock and multi-part jobs — arranging multiple part outlines efficiently across a sheet to minimize the material lost between parts. It isn't a general CNC billet concept; a single part machined from a solid block doesn't have a "nesting" decision to make the way a batch of flat-pattern parts cut from a sheet does. Material choice itself matters too, but the substitution logic has to run in the right order: the material still has to meet the part's performance requirements first. Only once a shortlist of materials clears that bar does it make sense to compare them on available billet sizes, how predictably each machines at the removal rates the job needs, and what the resulting chips are worth as segregated scrap. Swapping to a "more machinable" alloy that doesn't meet the part's actual requirements isn't a waste-reduction win. Lever 3: Strategic Machining (Toolpath and Process Planning) How the cutting itself is planned affects both direct material waste and the indirect waste from tool wear and rework. Efficient toolpath strategy — appropriate stepover, sensible roughing-to-finishing sequencing, avoiding unnecessary air-cutting or redundant passes — reduces both cycle time and the material removed less efficiently than it needs to be. Our guide on 5 CNC techniques to reduce waste in metal fabrication covers specific, actionable strategies at this level — smarter nesting, better blank sizing, intelligent toolpaths, optimized speeds, and simulation to catch problems before they become scrap. Lever 4: Tool Maintenance A dulling tool doesn't just cut less efficiently — it increases the risk of a part drifting out of tolerance or developing a poor surface finish, both of which can turn a nearly-finished part into scrap. Tracking tool wear against expected tool life, rather than running tools until they visibly fail, catches this before it produces bad parts. Our guide on tool wear detection and maintenance covers how to monitor this systematically rather than reactively. Lever 5: Waste Recycling What can't be avoided can often still be recovered. Metal chips have real scrap value and are commonly collected and recycled rather than landfilled — and for shops running enough volume, chip segregation by alloy meaningfully increases what that scrap is worth. Cutting fluid and coolant, often treated as a simple consumable, can be filtered, reconditioned, and reused rather than fully replaced on a fixed schedule. Our guide on zero-waste CNC strategies for recycling metal chips and coolant covers this specific piece of the waste picture — the recovery and recycling side, as distinct from the upstream prevention covered by the other four levers above. How to Prioritize These Five Levers Not every shop needs to tackle all five levers at once, and they aren't equally cheap to act on. A reasonable order to work through them: Check whether the billet or process itself can change first. Near-net-shape stock and process selection (Lever 2) are usually the single biggest lever available before any design or toolpath work happens. Then check whether the design is over-machining. A DFM review (Lever 1) catches unnecessary material and oversized stock allowances that would otherwise get machined away regardless of how efficient the toolpath is. Then reduce scrap and rework. Toolpath planning and tool maintenance (Levers 3 and 4) address the waste that comes from parts failing spec or requiring rework, which is often more expensive per part than raw material waste. Recover what's left. Recycling (Lever 5) is the last step because it deals with waste that's already unavoidable — chips and spent coolant that remain even after the first four levers are optimized. This order roughly matches how much control each lever has upstream of the actual cutting — the earlier a decision happens in this list, the more waste it prevents rather than merely recovers. What Not to Compromise When Reducing CNC Waste Treating waste reduction as purely a sustainability or compliance concern, separate from cost, undersells how directly it affects the bottom line. Every gram of scrap material is raw material that was purchased and then paid for again in machine time to remove — waste reduction is a cost optimization lever as much as an environmental one, and in most shops, the cost argument is what actually drives adoption. That said, waste reduction has a real failure mode worth naming directly: don't loosen functional tolerances, skip a necessary finishing pass, or lower a genuine quality requirement in the name of cutting material or cycle time. A part that comes back out of tolerance or fails in service because a step was cut to save material isn't a waste-reduction win — it's scrap with extra steps, and it usually costs more than the material it was meant to save. The "over-correcting" version of this mistake — tightening tolerances or adding excessive finishing passes in the name of "getting it right the first time" — is its mirror image, and can increase machining time and tool wear enough to offset whatever material savings were gained. (minaprem) If you've ever stood in front of a CNC machine or a manual lathe, you know that the cutting tool's geometry isn't just some arbitrary design. Every angle, edge, and surface has a job to do, and one of the most important of those is the rake angle . We've been running machines long enough to know that rake angle can make or break your surface finish, tool life, and machining efficiency. In this guide, we're going to walk you through what rake angle is, how it works, and how to choose the right one , without all the confusing textbook terms. The rake angle in a cutting tool is the angle between the tool\s rake face (the surface where the chip slides away) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. Think of it as how much your tool “leans” into or away from the cut: Positive rake angle: The Tool face leans forward toward the cut Negative rake angle: The Tool face leans backward away from the cut Why it matters: rake angle affects chip formation, cutting forces, tool wear, and even surface finish. Why Rake Angle is Critical in Machining (Istock) In real-world machining, even a small change in cutting tool rake angle can: Lower or increase cutting forces Improve or worsen surface finish Extend or shorten tool life Affect chip control and heat dissipation A good rake angle means the tool slices material efficiently. A poor one? It plows through the workpiece, causing chatter, heat, and early tool failure. A well-chosen rake angle can dramatically improve your part's surface finish. For more practical tips, see our guide on How to Improve Surface Finish in CNC Machining . Types of Rake Angle 1. Positive Rake Angle (ResearchGate) Tool face leans toward the cut. Advantages: Lower cutting forces Smoother surface finish Less heat Disadvantages: Weaker cutting edge (prone to chipping) Best for: Aluminum, brass, plastics, and soft steels. 2. Negative Rake Angle (ResearchGate) The tool face leans away from the cut. Advantages: Stronger cutting edge Can handle hard materials and interrupted cuts Durable at high speeds and temps Disadvantages: Higher cutting forces More heat generation Best for: Titanium, hardened steels, nickel alloys, anywhere tool strength is priority. 3. Zero Rake Angle (Minaprem) Neutral cutting edge, neither forward nor backward lean. Best for: General turning, moderate toughness, balanced performance. How to Get Rake Angle in a Cutting Tool There are two main ways we get rake angle: 1. Built into the Tool Geometry Carbide inserts, HSS tools, or form tools come with a pre-designed rake angle. You choose the right insert geometry for the job. 2. By Tool Setup or Holder Design Sometimes, the toolholder itself provides a rake (especially in turning tools or milling cutters). Tilting the tool in the machine can also alter the effective rake angle. If you're wondering "how to get rake angle" , the answer is really about choosing the right insert grade and holder combo for your material, and making sure your setup matches your machining goals. Practical Tips for Choosing the Right Rake Angle For soft materials: Go positive. You'll thank yourself for the smoother cuts and smaller forces. For hard or abrasive materials: Go negative. Your edge will last longer. For interrupted cuts (like milling a part with keyways or turning across drilled holes): negative rake is usually safer. Always match feed rate & spindle speed to your rake angle, a positive rake can chatter if you feed too slowly. Chip Control and Rake Angle (FK instrument) One thing many beginners miss is how rake angle affects chip shape: Positive rake: Thinner, more curled chips Negative rake: Thicker, more segmented chips If you're trying to get those perfect “6” or “9”-shaped chips for safety and chip evacuation, adjusting rake angle is one of your most powerful tools. Need help picking the right cutting tool rake angle for your material? Upload your CAD file here , and we'll help you choose the perfect tooling setup for maximum efficiency. FAQ 1. What is rake angle in a cutting tool? The rake angle is the angle between the cutting tool's rake face (where the chip flows) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. It controls how the tool enters the material, affects chip formation, cutting forces, and surface finish. 2. Why is rake angle important in machining? Rake angle directly impacts cutting efficiency, heat generation, and tool life. The right rake angle improves chip flow, reduces cutting forces, and helps you get a smoother finish. The wrong rake angle can cause tool wear, chatter, and poor part quality. 3. What is a negative rake angle and when should I use it? A negative rake angle means the cutting face leans away from the cut. It's best for hard, abrasive, or high-strength materials where tool edge durability matters more than ease of cutting. 4. What's the difference between positive and negative rake angles? Positive rake → Easier cutting, smoother finish, less heat, but weaker edge. Negative rake → Stronger edge, handles tough materials, but generates more cutting forces and heat. 5. How do you get the correct rake angle in machining? You can achieve a rake angle through the cutting tool's built-in geometry or by adjusting toolholder setup. Many CNC insert manufacturers specify the rake angle in their catalogs, so match it to your material and job type. 6. Does rake angle affect chip control? Yes! Positive rake angles create thin, curled chips, while negative rake angles produce thicker, more segmented chips. Adjusting rake angle can help prevent chip jamming and improve safety. 7. Can rake angle improve surface finish? Absolutely. A properly chosen rake angle slices the material instead of plowing it, resulting in a smoother, more accurate surface finish, especially on soft materials. Final Thoughts Rake angle isn't just a textbook term, it's a real-world lever you can pull to make machining faster, cleaner, and more cost-effective. If you've never paid attention to your rake angle before, start experimenting. You'll quickly see why it's one of the most important elements in cutting tool rake angle design and rake angle in machining performance. (minaprem) If you've ever stood in front of a CNC machine or a manual lathe, you know that the cutting tool's geometry isn't just some arbitrary design. Every angle, edge, and surface has a job to do, and one of the most important of those is the rake angle . We've been running machines long enough to know that rake angle can make or break your surface finish, tool life, and machining efficiency. In this guide, we're going to walk you through what rake angle is, how it works, and how to choose the right one , without all the confusing textbook terms. The rake angle in a cutting tool is the angle between the tool\s rake face (the surface where the chip slides away) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. Think of it as how much your tool “leans” into or away from the cut: Positive rake angle: The Tool face leans forward toward the cut Negative rake angle: The Tool face leans backward away from the cut Why it matters: rake angle affects chip formation, cutting forces, tool wear, and even surface finish. Why Rake Angle is Critical in Machining (Istock) In real-world machining, even a small change in cutting tool rake angle can: Lower or increase cutting forces Improve or worsen surface finish Extend or shorten tool life Affect chip control and heat dissipation A good rake angle means the tool slices material efficiently. A poor one? It plows through the workpiece, causing chatter, heat, and early tool failure. A well-chosen rake angle can dramatically improve your part's surface finish. For more practical tips, see our guide on How to Improve Surface Finish in CNC Machining . Types of Rake Angle 1. Positive Rake Angle (ResearchGate) Tool face leans toward the cut. Advantages: Lower cutting forces Smoother surface finish Less heat Disadvantages: Weaker cutting edge (prone to chipping) Best for: Aluminum, brass, plastics, and soft steels. 2. Negative Rake Angle (ResearchGate) The tool face leans away from the cut. Advantages: Stronger cutting edge Can handle hard materials and interrupted cuts Durable at high speeds and temps Disadvantages: Higher cutting forces More heat generation Best for: Titanium, hardened steels, nickel alloys, anywhere tool strength is priority. 3. Zero Rake Angle (Minaprem) Neutral cutting edge, neither forward nor backward lean. Best for: General turning, moderate toughness, balanced performance. How to Get Rake Angle in a Cutting Tool There are two main ways we get rake angle: 1. Built into the Tool Geometry Carbide inserts, HSS tools, or form tools come with a pre-designed rake angle. You choose the right insert geometry for the job. 2. By Tool Setup or Holder Design Sometimes, the toolholder itself provides a rake (especially in turning tools or milling cutters). Tilting the tool in the machine can also alter the effective rake angle. If you're wondering "how to get rake angle" , the answer is really about choosing the right insert grade and holder combo for your material, and making sure your setup matches your machining goals. Practical Tips for Choosing the Right Rake Angle For soft materials: Go positive. You'll thank yourself for the smoother cuts and smaller forces. For hard or abrasive materials: Go negative. Your edge will last longer. For interrupted cuts (like milling a part with keyways or turning across drilled holes): negative rake is usually safer. Always match feed rate & spindle speed to your rake angle, a positive rake can chatter if you feed too slowly. Chip Control and Rake Angle (FK instrument) One thing many beginners miss is how rake angle affects chip shape: Positive rake: Thinner, more curled chips Negative rake: Thicker, more segmented chips If you're trying to get those perfect “6” or “9”-shaped chips for safety and chip evacuation, adjusting rake angle is one of your most powerful tools. Need help picking the right cutting tool rake angle for your material? Upload your CAD file here , and we'll help you choose the perfect tooling setup for maximum efficiency. FAQ 1. What is rake angle in a cutting tool? The rake angle is the angle between the cutting tool's rake face (where the chip flows) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. It controls how the tool enters the material, affects chip formation, cutting forces, and surface finish. 2. Why is rake angle important in machining? Rake angle directly impacts cutting efficiency, heat generation, and tool life. The right rake angle improves chip flow, reduces cutting forces, and helps you get a smoother finish. The wrong rake angle can cause tool wear, chatter, and poor part quality. 3. What is a negative rake angle and when should I use it? A negative rake angle means the cutting face leans away from the cut. It's best for hard, abrasive, or high-strength materials where tool edge durability matters more than ease of cutting. 4. What's the difference between positive and negative rake angles? Positive rake → Easier cutting, smoother finish, less heat, but weaker edge. Negative rake → Stronger edge, handles tough materials, but generates more cutting forces and heat. 5. How do you get the correct rake angle in machining? You can achieve a rake angle through the cutting tool's built-in geometry or by adjusting toolholder setup. Many CNC insert manufacturers specify the rake angle in their catalogs, so match it to your material and job type. 6. Does rake angle affect chip control? Yes! Positive rake angles create thin, curled chips, while negative rake angles produce thicker, more segmented chips. Adjusting rake angle can help prevent chip jamming and improve safety. 7. Can rake angle improve surface finish? Absolutely. A properly chosen rake angle slices the material instead of plowing it, resulting in a smoother, more accurate surface finish, especially on soft materials. Final Thoughts Rake angle isn't just a textbook term, it's a real-world lever you can pull to make machining faster, cleaner, and more cost-effective. If you've never paid attention to your rake angle before, start experimenting. You'll quickly see why it's one of the most important elements in cutting tool rake angle design and rake angle in machining performance. Published Jul 30, 2025, updated Jul 28, 2025 5 min Threading a hole sounds simple, until you’re deciding between thread milling and tapping . Both methods are staples in CNC machining and manual operations, but they serve different purposes, machines, and tolerances. Whether you're threading aluminum, stainless steel, or titanium, choosing the wrong method can mean broken tools, scrapped parts, or wasted hours. Let’s break down the real differences between thread milling vs tapping , when to use one over the other, and how to choose the right tool for your part. What is Tapping? Tapping is the traditional method of creating internal threads by driving a tap, a hardened cutting tool, into a pre-drilled hole. It’s fast, easy to set up, and widely used in manual and CNC operations. There are three common types of taps: ● Hand taps – used manually with a T-handle ● Spiral point taps – best for through holes ● Spiral flute taps – best for blind holes Taps are typically specific to one thread size and pitch, which makes them convenient but rigid in flexibility. What is Thread Milling? Thread milling , on the other hand, uses a rotating tool called a thread mill to cut threads with a helical interpolation motion. The tool enters the hole and follows a spiral path to form the thread, using a CNC program to control pitch and depth. There are three types of thread mills: ● Single-point thread mills – extremely flexible for custom threads ● Multi-form thread mills – cut the full profile in one pass ● Indexable thread mills – ideal for large threads or production runs Thread milling may require more programming and setup time, but it shines in areas tapping simply can't reach. Thread Milling vs Tapping: Head-to-Head Comparison Let’s stack up thread milling vs tapping in the areas that matter most: Feature Tapping Thread Milling Speed Faster for high-volume production Slower, especially for large threads Tool Flexibility One tap per size/thread One thread mill can cut many sizes Material Suitability Risk of tap breakage in tough metals Better for hard-to-machine materials Thread Quality High-quality but fixed geometry Adjustable depth and excellent finish Chip Control Poor in blind holes Better evacuation and cleaner threads Cost Cheaper per tool Higher initial tool cost, lower long-term Thread Milling and Tapping in Different Materials When working with softer materials like aluminum or mild steel, tapping is fast and rarely problematic. But when dealing with: ● Stainless steel ● Tool steel ● Superalloys …thread milling provides better tool life and reduces the risk of tool breakage. This makes it a smart choice for aerospace, medical, and high-precision industries. CNC Programming Differences Tapping usually relies on a simple cycle (G84 for right-hand, G74 for left-hand tapping). Easy to program, minimal variables. Thread milling , on the other hand, requires: ● Circular interpolation (G02/G03) ● Depth control ● Helix angle programming While this adds complexity, modern CAM software and CNCs make it increasingly easier. Tool Life and Cost Considerations Taps wear out quickly in hard materials and can break, especially in blind holes with poor chip evacuation. Thread mills , although more expensive upfront, last longer and are more forgiving, especially if you’re threading near the bottom of a hole. Plus, if a thread mill breaks, you typically don’t lose the entire part. Is Thread Milling Better Than Tapping? It depends on your application. Tapping wins when: ● You're working in high-volume production ● Thread size and material are standard ● Speed and cost-per-hole are critical Thread milling is better when: ● You're threading expensive or difficult materials like Inconel or titanium ● You need flexibility in thread sizes or depths ● You want to avoid breaking taps in blind holes ● You're using CNC machines capable of helical interpolation So, is thread milling better than tapping ? In terms of flexibility and safety, yes. But in terms of speed and simplicity, tapping still holds the crown for everyday work. At JLCCNC , we specialize in precise, reliable threaded parts, no matter the size, material, or threading method. Whether you need help programming a thread milling cycle or want bulk tapping production , we’re here to help. Upload your design file and get a free quote here , we’ll recommend the best process for your job. Final Word: Which One Should You Use? Use tapping when: ● You need speed and low cost ● You’re working on large batches with consistent threads ● You have limited CNC capabilities Use thread milling when: ● You're working with tough or expensive materials ● Flexibility, precision, and thread quality matter ● You're threading blind holes or varying thread diameters Pro tip: If you’re threading critical parts, test both methods. A single broken tap can cost more than investing in a thread mill. Want More? Threading precision matters. Check out our guide on CNC tolerances and machining accuracy for a deeper understanding of how to control fit, finish, and dimensional repeatability. Whether you're working with tough materials, tight tolerances, or just want expert advice on choosing between thread milling and tapping , our CNC machining services have you covered. Upload your design file and get a free quote, let’s bring your part to life with accuracy and confidence. Types of Holes and CNC Hole Machining Explained In CNC machining, few operations challenge process control and tool stability as much as blind hole machining. A blind hole is a hole that terminates at a defined internal depth rather than breaking through the opposite surface. Because the cavity is enclosed at the bottom, chip evacuation, thermal behavior, tool wear, and dimensional accuracy become far more difficult to manage compared to through-hole machining. These constraints make blind holes indispensable yet technically demanding features across precision mechanical parts, sealed housings, consumer products, and structural components. When projects require consistently accurate blind hole drilling, tapping, or fine-tolerance cavity machining, J LCCNC provides reliable depth control , specialized tool paths, and clean internal finishes, supporting both prototypes and full production. What Is a Blind Hole? (Quora) A blind hole is defined by its closed end. Unlike a through hole, which passes entirely through a workpiece, a blind hole stops before reaching the opposite side. The bottom shape varies depending on the tool used: conventional drills produce conical bottoms, whereas flat-bottom drills and end mills generate planar surfaces suitable for precision assemblies or tapping. The engineering purpose of blind holes extends well beyond simply preventing penetration. In structural parts, maintaining a continuous opposite surface preserves rigidity, prevents stress risers, and helps sustain load paths. In pressurized or sealed systems—pneumatic housings, pump bodies, battery enclosures—blind holes prevent leakage of fluids or gases. In aesthetic or ergonomic products, they allow components to be fastened internally without exposing screw holes on the exterior. Blind holes essentially balance internal functionality with external appearance, mechanical strength, and environmental protection. Blind Hole vs Through Hole Through holes are straightforward to machine because chips naturally exit, tools experience less thermal stress, and depth accuracy is less sensitive. Blind holes demand precise programming—typically down to fractions of a millimeter—because any error may result in breakthrough. Through holes favor higher cutting speeds and simpler setups, whereas blind holes influence manufacturing costs due to slower feeds, peck cycles, coolant optimization, and bottom-clearance requirements. This difference in machining complexity explains why blind hole features often drive DFM (Design for Manufacturability) considerations. Types of Holes in CNC Machining Hole geometry in CNC machining reflects functional intent. Through holes support fasteners, shafts, dowel pins, and alignment features, making them ideal for high-speed fabrication. Countersunk holes allow screws to sit flush with the surface, maintaining flatness in precision mechanical surfaces. Counterbores accommodate socket-cap screws and create controlled seating planes for load-bearing joints. Within this landscape, blind holes occupy a specialized category. They enable internal threads, hidden fastening points, or mounting cavities that must not disturb the profile or sealing plane of the component. In industrial machinery, blind holes allow assembly without compromising fluid channels or structural ribs. In consumer electronics, they maintain the clean, uninterrupted outer surfaces expected from modern design. The choice between blind and through holes ultimately depends on the balance between manufacturability and functional necessity. Blind Hole Machining Explained (Science Direct) Blind hole machining is more complex than ordinary drilling because the tool must operate inside a confined cavity with no path for chips to escape. As the flutes fill with chips, heat rises sharply and causes accelerated tool wear or material hardening, especially in stainless steel and titanium. This is why blind hole drilling strategies emphasize controlled chip load, coolant access, and stable tool geometry. Drilling Blind Holes Standard twist drills are used for most metals, but they form a conical bottom that may not meet design requirements. When engineers need a flat-bottomed blind hole—for example, to optimize the thread engagement length or to improve seating conditions—a flat-bottom drill or end mill is applied. Peck drilling cycles become essential in deeper holes, where periodic retraction clears chips and reduces heat. In high-precision applications, depth is repeatedly verified using machine probing or tool setters to ensure no risk of breakthrough. Depth Control and Tool Selection Depth accuracy is one of the defining challenges in blind hole machining. CNC tools rely on tool length offsets, spindle probing, or laser measurement systems to maintain consistency. Carbide drills offer superior rigidity for deeper holes, while coatings such as TiAlN or AlTiN stabilize cutting edges under heat. The selected tool often reflects not only the material but also the hole’s final function—threaded, reamed, or used as a locating feature. Material Behavior in Blind Hole Drilling Aluminum machines easily but forms long, continuous chips that can clog a blind cavity unless chip-breaking geometries are used. Stainless steel hardens quickly under heat and demands strict lubrication control. Titanium concentrates heat at the cutting edge, often requiring through-tool coolant systems. Engineering plastics behave differently—they may melt or smear if spindle speeds are excessive. The interaction between tool, material, and confined cavity defines the entire machining strategy for blind holes. Blind Hole Tapping (Blind Hole Tap) (Science Direct) Blind hole tapping is one of the most technically sensitive procedures in CNC machining. Unlike through-hole tapping, where excess chips simply exit the opposite side, blind hole tapping traps chips at the bottom. If unmanaged, these chips compact and cause tap breakage. Bottoming Taps for Blind Holes A blind hole tap—usually a bottoming tap—features very little chamfer, enabling threads to form almost to the bottom of the cavity. This is crucial when the full thread depth is needed for load-bearing joints, especially in aerospace or automotive parts. Plug taps and taper taps have longer chamfers and are not suitable for holes where thread engagement must begin close to the bottom. Best Practices for Tapping Blind Holes Effective blind hole tapping relies on rigid tapping cycles, stable lubrication, and precise pilot hole sizing. In difficult materials, spiral-flute taps help extract chips upward, preventing compaction at the bottom of the hole. Thread milling is often chosen when the material is prone to chip welding or when the design requires extremely tight tolerance control. The entire process must anticipate torque spikes, potential chip packing, and sensitivity to tool wear. Designing Blind Holes for CNC Manufacturing Blind hole design affects machinability more than most engineers initially assume. Hole depth must align with available drill and tap geometries, ensuring that tools do not deflect excessively. The bottom clearance should reflect the type of threading operation planned, and thin walls around the hole must be avoided to prevent distortion during machining. Depth, Diameter, and Tolerance The ratio between hole depth and diameter heavily influences tool stability. Excessively deep blind holes increase the likelihood of tool vibration, poor chip evacuation, and dimensional variation. Tolerance selection must reflect not only fit and function but also the realities of machining inside a confined space. Surface finish is another consideration: smoother walls reduce thread friction, improve fastener performance, and reduce wear during repeated assembly cycles. FAQ What is the purpose of a blind hole? To enable internal mounting, threading, or functional cavities without penetrating the opposite surface, preserving structure, sealing integrity, or aesthetics. Why is blind hole machining more complex than through holes? Restricted chip flow, higher heat concentration, and tighter depth accuracy requirements. How are blind holes tapped successfully? With bottoming taps, rigid cycles, proper lubrication, and chip evacuation strategies such as spiral flutes or thread milling. What is blind hole drilling? A controlled-depth drilling process designed to terminate precisely before breakthrough. What is CNC Technology? CNC technology refers to the integrated use of software, control systems, and automated machinery to manage and execute precision manufacturing processes. In modern production environments, CNC technology functions as a core manufacturing platform—linking digital design data with machining operations, tool management, and quality control systems. Advantages of CNC Technology CNC technology offers a wide range of advantages that make it essential to modern manufacturing. By combining computer-controlled automation with high-performance machinery, CNC systems significantly improve manufacturing efficiency. They also enable superior quality and scalability across diverse industries. High Precision and Consistent Accuracy One of the most significant advantages of CNC technology is its ability to deliver extremely high precision. CNC technology can repeatedly produce components with tight tolerances that are difficult or impossible to achieve through manual machining. Once a program is validated, the same dimensions and surface quality can be maintained across thousands of parts, ensuring consistent accuracy even in complex geometries. This level of precision is especially critical in industries such as aerospace, automotive, medical devices, and electronics, where small dimensional deviations can affect performance, safety, or compliance with industry standards. Increased Production Efficiency CNC technology dramatically improves production efficiency by automating machining operations. Machines can run continuously with minimal operator intervention, reducing setup time and accelerating production cycles. Multi-axis CNC systems further enhance efficiency by completing multiple operations—such as milling, drilling, and contouring—in a single setup. Automated tool changes, optimized tool paths, and high-speed machining capabilities allow manufacturers to shorten lead times and respond quickly to changing production demands. Excellent Repeatability and Quality Control Repeatability is a core strength of CNC technology. Every part produced from the same CNC program is virtually identical, minimizing variation and reducing scrap rates. This repeatability simplifies quality control processes, as fewer manual inspections are required once a process is stabilized. CNC systems also integrate easily with in-process measurement and inspection technologies, enabling real-time quality monitoring and early detection of deviations before defects occur. Material and Design Versatility CNC technology supports a wide range of materials, including metals, plastics, composites, and engineered alloys. From aluminum and stainless steel to advanced polymers and titanium, CNC machines can be optimized to handle different cutting characteristics and surface finish requirements. A common example is aluminum CNC machining , which is widely used due to aluminum’s excellent machinability and strength-to-weight ratio. In addition, CNC technology enables the machining of complex shapes, internal features, and intricate contours that would be extremely time-consuming or impractical with conventional methods. This design freedom allows engineers to innovate without being limited by manufacturing constraints. Scalability from Prototyping to Mass Production Another key advantage of CNC technology is its scalability. The same CNC setup can be used for rapid prototyping, small-batch production, and high-volume manufacturing with minimal modification. Design changes can be implemented quickly by updating the digital program rather than retooling entire production lines. This flexibility is particularly valuable for startups, R&D teams, and manufacturers operating in fast-moving markets where product iterations are frequent. Reduced Labor Dependency and Improved Safety By automating machining tasks, CNC technology reduces reliance on manual labor and lowers the risk of human error. Operators are less exposed to cutting tools and moving machine components, resulting in a safer working environment. Modern CNC systems also feature built-in safety controls, error detection, and machine monitoring functions that further protect both personnel and equipment while maintaining stable production. Cost Efficiency Over the Product Lifecycle While CNC machines require an initial investment, they offer long-term cost advantages. Reduced material waste, lower rework rates, shorter production times, and improved machine utilization all contribute to a lower cost per part over the product lifecycle. For manufacturers seeking consistent quality, predictable output, and efficient resource usage, CNC technology represents a cost-effective solution that supports sustainable growth. Applications of CNC Technology in Manufacturing CNC technology has a wide range of applications across industries due to its ability to deliver high precision, consistency, and production efficiency. From large-scale industrial manufacturing to rapid prototyping, CNC technology continues to expand as materials, software, and machine capabilities evolve. Applications in Metalworking CNC milling machines, lathes, and laser cutters handle metals like aluminum, steel, and titanium with unmatched precision. These machines reduce manual labor, minimize errors, and allow for complex shapes that meet rigorous industry standards. In metalworking industries where tolerance control and material consistency are critical, CNC technology enables reliable production of complex metal components at scale. Applications in Plastics and Woodworking Beyond metals, CNC routers can cut, engrave, and shape plastic components or wood panels with high accuracy. Routers are typically used for wood and plastic materials, while milling machines are better suited for metal machining due to their rigidity and cutting capabilities. Manufacturers can efficiently produce prototypes and mass-produced items, lowering production costs and turnaround times. Industrial Applications Industries such as automotive, aerospace, electronics, energy, and heavy machinery rely on CNC systems to produce structural components, housings, brackets, and precision parts. CNC machining ensures tight tolerances, repeatability, and high reliability for critical components. Prototyping and Small Batch Production Rapid prototyping and small-batch CNC production allow engineers to quickly transform digital designs into functional prototypes, enabling faster design validation, iterative testing, and reduced time-to-market. Innovative Uses in Various Industries Advanced applications such as multi-axis cutting, hybrid additive-subtractive manufacturing, and complex 3D contour machining expand possibilities in medical devices, architecture, and custom design. CNC Machine Technology Types of CNC Machines CNC machine technology includes milling machines, lathes, routers, plasma cutters, and laser engraving systems. Each type serves a specific function, from cutting and drilling to shaping and engraving, meeting diverse manufacturing needs. How CNC Machines Work CNC machines operate by translating digital designs into precise machining actions through integrated control systems. This enables highly accurate and repeatable production while minimizing material waste and optimizing workflow efficiency. Maintenance and Optimization Proper maintenance of CNC machines is essential for long-term performance. Regular calibration, tool replacement, and software updates optimize machine efficiency and prevent downtime. Skilled operators can further enhance productivity by choosing the right tooling and machining parameters. Industrial CNC Technology Automation in Large-Scale Production Industrial CNC technology enables full automation of production lines. Large-scale manufacturing can run continuously with minimal human supervision, improving throughput and reducing labor costs. Integration with Industrial Processes CNC technology integrates seamlessly with industrial processes such as assembly, quality inspection, and material handling. This integration allows for smarter factories, streamlined workflows, and higher overall efficiency. Case Studies Industries adopting industrial CNC technology have reported reduced production errors, faster turnaround times, and improved product consistency. For example, automotive suppliers use CNC machines to produce engine components with precise tolerances, enhancing vehicle performance and reliability. Manufacturing and Prototyping Services Service providers offer CNC machining for both prototypes and mass production. Maintenance and Support Services Many CNC technology service providers also offer ongoing maintenance, troubleshooting, and training. This ensures clients can maintain efficient operations, extend machine lifespan, and minimize production delays. Future developments will not only improve precision and productivity but also fundamentally reshape how factories operate, how products are designed, and how manufacturers compete in global markets. Smart CNC and AI Integration The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with CNC systems is transforming machining from reactive automation into predictive and adaptive manufacturing. AI-powered algorithms can analyze historical machining data. They automatically optimize tool paths, reduce cycle times, and minimize tool wear. Machine learning models are increasingly used to detect subtle signs of tool degradation or misalignment before they cause defects. In aerospace and medical device manufacturing, where tolerances are extremely tight, AI-assisted CNC tool path optimization is already being adopted to ensure consistency and precision across complex geometries. Over time, smart CNC machines will be able to adjust cutting strategies in real time, self-correcting for material inconsistencies and dynamic load variations without human intervention. Sensors embedded in CNC equipment collect real-time data on temperature, vibration, spindle load, and tool life. This data, streamed through secure networks, feeds into centralized manufacturing execution systems (MES) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems to support real-time monitoring and informed decision-making. Connected CNC machines can automatically schedule maintenance based on actual usage patterns, reducing unplanned downtime. In facilities with multiple machines producing different parts, IoT connectivity enhances workflow coordination, material tracking, and quality control, leading to higher operational efficiency and lower production costs. Advanced composites, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) , and next-generation polymers have unique machining requirements. High-entropy alloys are composed of multiple principal elements in near-equal proportions, offering exceptional strength, wear resistance, and thermal stability. These materials are increasingly used in aerospace and energy applications, where CNC machining must precisely control cutting forces and heat generation to maintain part integrity. These hybrid processes allow complex internal structures to be built additively and then finished with high-precision CNC cutting, making them ideal for lightweight aerospace components and customized medical implants. Augmented reality (AR) tools will support setup, training, and maintenance by overlaying digital instructions directly onto physical machinery. Technicians wearing AR headsets will be guided step-by-step through complex calibration or repair processes, reducing training time and lowering the risk of error. Furthermore, virtual simulation environments will allow engineers to preview machining operations before any material is cut. This not only helps validate designs but also ensures that tooling and fixturing are optimized for efficiency and safety. It enables complex machining, reduces errors, and accelerates production cycles. Be Part of the PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest! by: PCBWay Sep 03,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News We are glad to announce that PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest has arrived. Prior to this, PCBWay successfully held six design contests. In each contest, we saw many eye-catching projects shared by outstanding and creative electronic engineers and enthusiasts. PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest will continue the previous purpose, which is to encourage more and more people to explore the charm of electronic design and participate in it. PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest: https://www.pcbway.com/activity/7th-project-design-contest.html . In this contest, in addition to the two themes of Electronic Project and Mechanical Project that have appeared before, we also introduced STM32 Project, hoping to give designers more room to perform. The contest will start on September 2nd, 2024, and project submissions will be accepted until January 19th, 2025. After this, the judging phase will begin, and the final winners will be announced on the PCBWay Blog on March 10th, 2025. Two ways to participate in the contest: Go to the contest page, find the Participate Now button and click it. In this case, the submitted project will automatically be entered into the competition; participants only need to select the theme of entry. Please note that if you are submitting a mechanical project, please switch to the CNC |3D Printing Project page. After filling in all the project information, simply click "Submit" at the bottom of the page. Go to the SharedProject Community ( https://www.pcbway.com/project/shareproject/ ) and click Create a project. Select the theme you are going to participate in. Similarly, if you are submitting a mechanical project, please switch to the CNC |3D Printing Project page. Hint: Sharing complete project files, including Gerber, BOM, Centroid file, schematics, 3D files, and so on will increase the chances of receiving a higher score. Awards and corresponding prizes: The First Prize : 1 winner, $1500 Cash + $200 Coupon + A Palm-sized Robot Dog*1 The Second Prize : 2 winners, $1000 Cash + $100 Coupon + Raspberry Pi 5 4GB *1 The Third Prize : 3 winners, $500 Cash + $50 Coupon + OpenMV4 H7 R2 Cam Smart Camera *1 Popular Design Prize : 10 winners, $100 Cash + $20 Coupon + $10 3D Printing Coupon + Multimeter ZTY890DPro *1 Participation Prize : Raspberry Pi Pico * 1 STM32 Great Project Prize : Six-Claw Multifunctional Aluminum Alloy Soldering Table *1 For more detailed information about the contest, please refer to: https://www.pcbway.com/activity/7th-project-design-contest.html . If there are any questions or suggestions, feel free to leave a comment below.We wish you the best of luck and look forward to your innovative designs! Verify Now Blog > Corporate Social Responsibility of PCBWay Corporate Social Responsibility of PCBWay by: PCBWay May 30,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News PCBWay recognizes the significant role it plays within the supply chain and broader society, along with the potential impact of its operations. To this end, we have established and strictly enforce the following principles, which not only govern our own conduct but also set clear expectations for our partners. Our goal is to ensure full legal and regulatory compliance, promote long-term sustainability, and generate a positive impact on society. Human Rights and Labor Protection No employment of individuals below the legal working age; all forms of forced or bonded labor are strictly prohibited. Discrimination and harassment in the workplace are not tolerated; an inclusive work environment for persons with disabilities is encouraged. Employees must be provided with fair compensation and reasonable rest periods, and their rights to freedom of association and collective bargaining must be respected. Business Ethics and Compliance Offering, promising, soliciting, or accepting any form of bribery is strictly prohibited; effective conflict of interest management and whistleblowing mechanisms must be in place. All financial and business records must accurately, completely, and truthfully reflect the underlying transactions. Full compliance with international sanctions, export controls, and other applicable laws and regulations is required. Supply Chain Responsibility and Sustainable Procurement PCBWay and its partners are required to extend the principles outlined in this document to all levels of entities within the supply chain. Priority should be given to selecting partners that are legally compliant, socially responsible, and committed to sustainable development. Identify social, labor, and environmental risks related to operations, and develop corresponding control and mitigation measures. Encourage partners to prioritize local sourcing to support regional economic development and job creation. Environmental Protection and Workplace Safety Actively implement environmental protection measures and continuously promote energy conservation and emission reduction; Ensure that all waste and hazardous materials are disposed of in accordance with relevant laws and regulations. The procurement or use of prohibited materials is not allowed. Provide employees with a safe working environment and health support mechanisms to prevent occupational injuries and health risks. PCBWay has fully adopted the DHL GoGreen transportation service in 2025 to reduce carbon emissions in the supply chain and promote the development of a green supply chain, with an initial target of reducing emissions by 30%. Information Protection and Transparent Governance Establish a comprehensive security system to strictly protect the confidentiality of customer data, drawings, and other business information. Comply with relevant laws and regulations to safeguard the personal data of customers and employees. Ensure that financial records are true, accurate, and complete, and prohibit any illegal activities. PCBWay will ensure the implementation of the above principles in actual cooperation and reserves the right to take action against any violations. To this end, we have established and strictly enforce the following principles, which not only govern our own conduct but also set clear expectations for our partners. Our goal is to ensure full legal and regulatory compliance, promote long-term sustainability, and generate a positive impact on society. Human Rights and Labor Protection No employment of individuals below the legal working age; all forms of forced or bonded labor are strictly prohibited. Discrimination and harassment in the workplace are not tolerated; an inclusive work environment for persons with disabilities is encouraged. Employees must be provided with fair compensation and reasonable rest periods, and their rights to freedom of association and collective bargaining must be respected. Business Ethics and Compliance Offering, promising, soliciting, or accepting any form of bribery is strictly prohibited; effective conflict of interest management and whistleblowing mechanisms must be in place. All financial and business records must accurately, completely, and truthfully reflect the underlying transactions. Full compliance with international sanctions, export controls, and other applicable laws and regulations is required. Supply Chain Responsibility and Sustainable Procurement PCBWay and its partners are required to extend the principles outlined in this document to all levels of entities within the supply chain. Priority should be given to selecting partners that are legally compliant, socially responsible, and committed to sustainable development. Identify social, labor, and environmental risks related to operations, and develop corresponding control and mitigation measures. Encourage partners to prioritize local sourcing to support regional economic development and job creation. Environmental Protection and Workplace Safety Actively implement environmental protection measures and continuously promote energy conservation and emission reduction; Ensure that all waste and hazardous materials are disposed of in accordance with relevant laws and regulations. The procurement or use of prohibited materials is not allowed. Provide employees with a safe working environment and health support mechanisms to prevent occupational injuries and health risks. PCBWay has fully adopted the DHL GoGreen transportation service in 2025 to reduce carbon emissions in the supply chain and promote the development of a green supply chain, with an initial target of reducing emissions by 30%. Information Protection and Transparent Governance Establish a comprehensive security system to strictly protect the confidentiality of customer data, drawings, and other business information. Comply with relevant laws and regulations to safeguard the personal data of customers and employees. Ensure that financial records are true, accurate, and complete, and prohibit any illegal activities. PCBWay will ensure the implementation of the above principles in actual cooperation and reserves the right to take action against any violations. Note: Regarding why your social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number is needed when shipping, please check out this official article for explanation: Why is an overseas supplier asking for my social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number? ============================================================================================== by the way： Importers - Why is an overseas supplier asking for my social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number? When an individual or company purchases goods from an overseas supplier, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) considers them the ultimate importer. The ultimate importer can clear the goods or have a Customs Broker clear them on their behalf. If the supplier hires a carrier that provides door to door service, the carrier service usually has brokers in their supply chain to clear the goods on behalf of the ultimate importer. If a formal entry is required, CBP regulations require the broker to put the ultimate importer's identification number on the CBP Form 7501- Entry Summary. The ultimate importer's identification number is either the Employers Identification Number (EIN) tax identification number assigned by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) or the importer's social security number. The EIN is issued for the purpose of tax administration and are not intended for participation in any other activities (e.g., tax lien auction or sales, lotteries). For additional information about EIN, please visit the IRS web page "Apply for an Employer Identification (EIN) Online." Goods are usually cleared informally when they are for personal use, under $2500 in value, and are not in commercial quantities. A formal entry is usually required for commercial importations valued over $2,500. Because many foreign merchants are aware that CBP requires an identification number for the ultimate importer for formal entries, they will often request the purchaser's social security number to include on export documents that the broker will subsequently rely on to prepare the CBP entry. It should be noted that paperwork for goods sent by courier service does ask for an importer number, whether the import qualifies for an informal entry or not. Courier services file CBP entries electronically, and the software system they use requires an identification number to be provided for the recipient of the goods. If an identification number is not provided, the courier service is required to file a paper entry, which is extremely time-consuming and in the world of "Overnight Delivery" not practical. The end result is that most courier services will not accept packages for international delivery to U.S. residents if a recipient's identification number is not provided by the shipper. Goods sent through the international postal service that are under $2500 in value generally do not require an importer number to be cleared through CBP. It’s Trickier Than You Think. But because of an ever-changing patchwork of trade rules, not every product will be charged an astronomical tariff, trade lawyers, customs brokers and importers say. In some cases, tariffs will pile on other tariffs. In other instances, they can reduce costs, while other times they can cancel out new ones. The new 125 percent rate that President Trump imposed will in many cases be added on top of long-existing duties. There are four main categories of tariffs that are imposed on goods from China. After taking the aforementioned actions, the Parties will establish a mechanism to continue discussions about economic and trade relations. The representative from the Chinese side for these discussions will be He Lifeng, Vice Premier of the State Council, and the representatives from the U.S. side will be Scott Bessent, Secretary of the Treasury, and Jamieson Greer, United States Trade Representative. These discussions may be conducted alternately in China and the United States, or a third country upon agreement of the Parties. As required, the two sides may conduct working-level consultations on relevant economic and trade issues. https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2025/05/joint-statement-on-u-s-china-economic-and-trade-meeting-in-geneva/ Updated on April 25th **Presidential Executive Order on Tariff Adjustments for Chinese Goods** On April 8, 2025 (local time), U.S. President Donald Trump issued an executive order announcing the following tariff measures on goods originating from China (including Hong Kong, China): 1. **Elimination of De Minimis Exemption for Chinese-origin Goods** 2. **Additional 125%+20% (If it is the category under 9903.01.32 or 9903.01.33, the tariff exemption is 125%) Tariff on High-value Chinese Goods** 3.Fedex Official: For B2C shipments, a valid FedEx account number is required. 4.If the product falls under HTS categories 9903.01.32 or 9903.01.33, it qualifies for a 125% tariff exemption. However, DHL’s customs declaration system may inaccurately apply or fail to recognize the 125% exemption. If the recipient finds that the product is indeed eligible for the exemption but the 125% duty relief was not applied, they must file a dispute with DHL immediately, as there is a strict deadline for appeals. By the time the sender notices the issue, the appeal window may have already closed. Note: Regarding why your social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number is needed when shipping, please check out this official article for explanation: Why is an overseas supplier asking for my social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number? ============================================================================================== by the way： Importers - Why is an overseas supplier asking for my social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number? When an individual or company purchases goods from an overseas supplier, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) considers them the ultimate importer. The ultimate importer can clear the goods or have a Customs Broker clear them on their behalf. If the supplier hires a carrier that provides door to door service, the carrier service usually has brokers in their supply chain to clear the goods on behalf of the ultimate importer. If a formal entry is required, CBP regulations require the broker to put the ultimate importer's identification number on the CBP Form 7501- Entry Summary. The ultimate importer's identification number is either the Employers Identification Number (EIN) tax identification number assigned by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) or the importer's social security number. The EIN is issued for the purpose of tax administration and are not intended for participation in any other activities (e.g., tax lien auction or sales, lotteries). For additional information about EIN, please visit the IRS web page "Apply for an Employer Identification (EIN) Online." Goods are usually cleared informally when they are for personal use, under $2500 in value, and are not in commercial quantities. A formal entry is usually required for commercial importations valued over $2,500. Because many foreign merchants are aware that CBP requires an identification number for the ultimate importer for formal entries, they will often request the purchaser's social security number to include on export documents that the broker will subsequently rely on to prepare the CBP entry. It should be noted that paperwork for goods sent by courier service does ask for an importer number, whether the import qualifies for an informal entry or not. Courier services file CBP entries electronically, and the software system they use requires an identification number to be provided for the recipient of the goods. If an identification number is not provided, the courier service is required to file a paper entry, which is extremely time-consuming and in the world of "Overnight Delivery" not practical. The end result is that most courier services will not accept packages for international delivery to U.S. residents if a recipient's identification number is not provided by the shipper. Goods sent through the international postal service that are under $2500 in value generally do not require an importer number to be cleared through CBP. It’s Trickier Than You Think. But because of an ever-changing patchwork of trade rules, not every product will be charged an astronomical tariff, trade lawyers, customs brokers and importers say. In some cases, tariffs will pile on other tariffs. In other instances, they can reduce costs, while other times they can cancel out new ones. The new 125 percent rate that President Trump imposed will in many cases be added on top of long-existing duties. There are four main categories of tariffs that are imposed on goods from China. Verify Now Blog > Meet PCBWay at EPTECH 2026 in Calgary, Canada Meet PCBWay at EPTECH 2026 in Calgary, Canada by: Mila Oct 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News PCBWay is pleased to announce our participation in EPTECH 2026 – Calgary, part of Canada's national electronics trade show series. Join us on October 27, 2026, at the Best Western Premier Calgary Plaza Hotel & Conference Centre to connect with our team and explore manufacturing solutions for your electronic projects. Visit PCBWay at EPTECH Calgary 2026 Event: EPTECH 2026 – Calgary Date: October 27, 2026 Location: Best Western Premier Calgary Plaza Hotel & Conference Centre, Calgary, Canada PCBWay Booth: To be announced Stop by our booth to meet the PCBWay team, discuss your project requirements, and learn how our services can support your next development or manufacturing project. From Electronic Design to Product Manufacturing Turning an idea into a finished product often involves multiple stages, from circuit development and prototyping to mechanical fabrication and final assembly. PCBWay helps customers manage these steps with a broad range of engineering and manufacturing capabilities. Our PCB Design Service supports projects from schematic design and PCB layout to electronic product development. For customers who already have design files, we provide PCB fabrication and assembly services to help bring their designs to life. Beyond electronics, PCBWay also offers CNC machining, sheet metal fabrication, 3D printing, and injection molding. These services help customers develop custom enclosures, mechanical components, and functional prototypes, making it easier to coordinate different manufacturing needs throughout product development. Whether you are testing an early concept, improving an existing design, or preparing for production, PCBWay can support your project with flexible manufacturing options. EPTECH brings together electronics industry professionals, suppliers, and innovators, creating opportunities to exchange ideas and build new connections. If you are attending EPTECH 2026 in Calgary, we look forward to meeting you and discussing how PCBWay can help turn your ideas into reality. See you in Calgary! Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Join us Wanna be a dedicated PCBWay writer? We definately look forward to having you with us.
