Verify Now Blog > Meet PCBWay at Electronica 2026 in Munich, Germany Meet PCBWay at Electronica 2026 in Munich, Germany by: Mila Oct 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News PCBWay is excited to announce our participation in Electronica 2026, one of the leading international trade fairs for the electronics industry. Join us in Munich, Germany, from November 10 to 13, 2026, to explore PCB manufacturing, electronic assembly, and engineering solutions for your projects. Visit PCBWay at Hall A1 – Booth 559 We welcome engineers, designers, businesses, and electronics enthusiasts to visit our booth and learn more about PCBWay's services. Whether you are developing a new electronic product, building prototypes, or preparing for production, our team looks forward to discussing your project requirements and exploring how we can support your ideas. Event Details Event: Electronica 2026 Date: November 10–13, 2026 Location: Messe München, Munich, Germany PCBWay Booth: Hall A1 – 559 Discover PCBWay's Services PCBWay provides a wide range of manufacturing and engineering services to support electronic product development, from initial concepts and prototypes to production. PCB Manufacturing: Custom printed circuit boards in various specifications, including multilayer, HDI, flexible, and rigid-flex PCBs. PCB Assembly: Turnkey and partial PCB assembly services, including component sourcing, SMT assembly, through-hole assembly, and functional testing. PCB Design Service: Professional schematic design, PCB layout, and complete electronic product development support. CNC Machining and Sheet Metal Fabrication: Custom mechanical parts and enclosures for electronic devices, prototypes, and production applications. 3D Printing and Injection Molding: Rapid prototyping and custom plastic parts to help transform product concepts into physical components. By bringing these capabilities together, PCBWay helps customers simplify their development process and coordinate multiple manufacturing needs through one partner. Electronica brings together professionals from across the electronics industry, providing an opportunity to exchange ideas, explore new technologies, and build valuable connections. If you are attending Electronica 2026, stop by the PCBWay booth at Hall A1 – 559. We look forward to meeting you in Munich and discussing how PCBWay can help bring your electronic projects to life. See you at Electronica 2026 ! Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Join us Wanna be a dedicated PCBWay writer? We definately look forward to having you with us. Meet PCBWay at electronica 2024! by: PCBWay Oct 18,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Once again, we welcome the famous technology event electronica in Munich, Germany! Since the first exhibition was held in 1964, electronica has gradually grown and now covers the entire world of electronics, including the micro- and nano-worlds of semiconductor and micro systems technology, as well as measurement and sensor technology, display technology and vehicle electronics, etc., which is the best choice for any technology enthusiasts and industry practitioners. PCBWay has participated in theelectronica many times and has received a warm response every time. At the exhibition, everyone has the opportunity to get close to our various products and fully evaluate the performance and quality of our products, which is far beyond the scope of online communication. On-site interaction gives us the opportunity to answer everyone's questions in a timely manner and help them understand the products more comprehensively, thereby accelerating the process of cooperation. Therefore, after the exhibition, we not only strengthened our cooperation with existing customers, but also successfully attracted the attention of many new potential partners. PCBWay will certainly not be absent from this year's exhibition.In addition, in order to give everyone a better exhibition experience and also to show how much importance PCBWay attaches to this exhibition, this year we made some innovations: Time: 2024.11.12-2024.11.15 Location: Trade Fair Center Messe München, Germany PCBWay Booth No.: A1.163 Highlights: Color- printed Boards In addition to the PCB series products, 3D printed parts and sheet metal parts that we have been displaying in the past, we will also bring the latest color-printed board samples. This new product has attracted the attention and interest of many customers, so we hope to take this opportunity to let everyone experience the excellent effect and quality of the color-printed board in person. New Booth We focused on designing the on-site booth as well. We expanded the booth area to 5m x 14m, providing a larger activity space, and also improved the sophistication of various details, in order to make the overall atmosphere more professional and make everyone's visiting experience more comfortable. The final booth design renderings are as follows: Gifts We will also bring some small gifts to the exhibition, including water cups, neck masks, and T-shirts. Welcome to come and get them! Map: Also, we've prepared some free tickets, click the link and apply for them! https://tickets.messe-muenchen.de/MM/ELE24/Register/PCBWay_2024 Sorry, the 100+ current tickets are "sold out". We welcome you to our booth to receive gifts PCBWay will continue the past successful experience, bring more innovative products and solutions. We welcome you to visit our booth and witness PCBWay's innovation and growth! We’ve got everything ready, just wait for your arrival. ;) Exhibition Moments Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Join us Wanna be a dedicated PCBWay writer? We definately look forward to having you with us. Thank you to all participants for bringing your creativity, passion, and engineering expertise to life to celebrate 12 years of innovation with PCBWay! 1. Prize: $200 PCBWay Coupon 3. Second Prize (2 Winners) Design Name: Sci-Fi Badge Author: @Juan Carlos jsbalanzar Description: Breathing LED living tech badge with lamp charger RFID customization. Prize: $200 PCBWay Coupon Design Name: Neon Marquee Author: @Guiye Perez Bongiovanni Description: 2-layer 1.6mm PCB badge with green LEDs and ATtiny85 firmware. Prize: $200 PCBWay Coupon Congratulations to all the winners! Prizes and coupons will be issued soon. We want to express our gratitude to every designer, maker, and voter who participated and made the PCBWay 12th Anniversary celebration so remarkable. Stay tuned for our upcoming contests and events! Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad by: Anson Apr 01,2022 Posted in News Kicad PCB design Send your layout to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. Have you ever thought that when you complete the design on KiCad, you can place an order on pcbway with just one click? Now this idea is finally achieved (it's not an April Fool's joke). When you click PCBWay Plug-in button on Kicad, we will export these files in your project ( Please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin released at 2026 )： 1.Gerber files in correct format for production 2.IPC-Netlist file 3.Bom-file that includes all information of components 4.Pick and Place-file used in assembly You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files( usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before the production. Note:We have updated plugin for Kicad 10,you could also place assembly order directly now. But we need to get the component "Manufacture Part Number". Please confirm you run the "Update Board from Schematic" and install the latest version of the plugin. ﻿ Installation from the official KiCad repositories Just open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the KiCad main menu an install the "PCBWay Plug-in for KiCad" plugin from the selection list. Manual installation You can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Plug-in-for-Kicad , then open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About Bom We can get all information of components used in your design ( please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin) . In order to speed up the quotation of components, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) You just need to add the properties in your schematic like the picture shows: As a sponsor of KiCad, we will always support its development. Note: Thanks to the open source community. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad by: Anson Apr 01,2022 Posted in News Kicad PCB design Send your layout to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. Have you ever thought that when you complete the design on KiCad, you can place an order on pcbway with just one click? Now this idea is finally achieved (it's not an April Fool's joke). When you click PCBWay Plug-in button on Kicad, we will export these files in your project ( Please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin released at 2026 )： 1.Gerber files in correct format for production 2.IPC-Netlist file 3.Bom-file that includes all information of components 4.Pick and Place-file used in assembly You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files( usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before the production. Note:We have updated plugin for Kicad 10,you could also place assembly order directly now. But we need to get the component "Manufacture Part Number". Please confirm you run the "Update Board from Schematic" and install the latest version of the plugin. ﻿ Installation from the official KiCad repositories Just open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the KiCad main menu an install the "PCBWay Plug-in for KiCad" plugin from the selection list. Manual installation You can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Plug-in-for-Kicad , then open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About Bom We can get all information of components used in your design ( please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin) . In order to speed up the quotation of components, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) You just need to add the properties in your schematic like the picture shows: As a sponsor of KiCad, we will always support its development. Note: Thanks to the open source community. Since we are not skilled enough to edit on github at the moment, any feedback or questions please contact with anson@pcbway.com Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Join us Wanna be a dedicated PCBWay writer? We definately look forward to having you with us. Unlock Color PCB Printing with PCBWay! by: PCBWay Mar 08,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Color PCB Printing PCBWay Service Nowadays, traditional PCB printing technology can no longer meet the aesthetic requirements of modern circuit board production. To better fulfill customers' design needs, we are pleased to announce that PCBWay has introduced UV printing equipment. This equipment utilizes UV-curable inks to achieve high-quality image printing on various materials, including fiberglass boards, metal substrates, ceramic substrates, flexible boards, and rigid-flex boards. Entrance https://www.pcbway.com/orderonline.aspx Prerequisites for Ordering Maximum size for a single piece: 270*470MM; Selection of background soldermask color required. Design Specifications Drill holes, traces, soldermasks, and outline designs must comply with specifications. Avoid placing colored characters in areas with solder mask openings, such as surface-mount pads or through-hole pads. What kind of files should be provided for color printing? Method One : Draw colored characters on the silkscreen layer of the Gerber and provide reference pictures. For example: Method Two : If you include information about colored silkscreen in the Gerber layer, each individual color must have its own layer. If there is only one layer, we can only print one color. [This method is not recommended] . If you need to print in multiple colors, we recommend using method One and providing us with a reference picture. 4.Please send the images you want to print on the PCB in the following formats: AI, PDF, JPEG, PNG, TIFF, etc., and indicate your desired printing location on the board. 5.If the image contains a QR code, please ensure that the QR code can be accurately scanned and recognized. Note : If you choose UV printing Multi-color, we will use matte UV color printing by default. When designing the colored characters on the bottom layer, be careful not to design the colored characters as mirrored inverses. (The process of color printing is different from that of standard PCB silkscreen printing. When printing colorful characters on the bottom layer, they are printed with the bottom layer of the PCB facing up.) For situations where the entire top or bottom side requires full-color printing, regardless of the solder mask color you choose, we will use a white solder mask on the full-color printed side and then proceed with the color printing. This is for a better printing effect. Please upload the print image, positioning image, and Gerber in one compressed file. By providing a clear positioning image and necessary instructions, you can assist PCBWay in accurately determining and achieving the desired printing position. Matte UV Color Printing vs. Glossy UV Color Printing Matte ink does not increase the overall thickness, and the PCB's appearance looks smooth. Glossy ink increases the overall thickness and may affect the soldering of component pads. The appearance is beautiful but uneven. Features Adopting UV-LED lamp curing, which enables instant drying, can significantly enhances production efficiency. UV printing technology employs UV-curable inks, ensuring firm and clear printing information resistant to fading, thus enhancing product identification and aesthetics. The normal print survives SMT reflow. UV printing technology can present images in various colors and styles, meeting customers' personalized requirements. Professional industrial-grade UV printers support high-precision printing, delivering exquisite results whether on flat panels or rolled materials. Unlike traditional printing methods, UV printing does not produce volatile organic compounds during the production process, ensuring air quality in the production workshop and providing employees with a safer and healthier working environment. FAQ on UV Printing: Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with water? Yes, it can be cleaned with water. Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with alcohol? It is more difficult to clean after being exposed to alcohol and baked (currently, the board undergoes a short baking process after UV printing). However, with increased contact time with alcohol and vigorous scrubbing, it can be removed. This also depends on whether the UV is on the copper surface or the solder mask surface. How hard is the UV printed surface (sensitivity to scratches)? The UV surface is not sensitive to scratches. However, compared to the solder mask, it is less scratch-resistant because UV printing is ink that is sprayed on and is relatively thin. Welcome to give it a try if you're interested! Besides, PCBWay will continue to enhance its manufacturing capabilities to bring more choices and personalized services to customers in the future. Verify Now Blog > Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips by: Mila Sep 30,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout analog vs digital circuits analog and digital circuits analog circuits digital circuits mixed signal PCB design We often say that the world of chips consists of only 0s and 1s. But more accurately, digital circuits use defined voltage ranges to represent discrete logic states, while the real world is clearly not like that. Human voices have different volumes, light has different levels of brightness, temperature changes continuously, and radio waves do not simply jump between 0 V and 1 V. So here is the question: If CPUs mainly process digital data, how can a smartphone hear sound, capture photos, connect to a cellular network, and charge its battery? The answer lies in three types of chips: digital chips, analog chips, and mixed-signal chips. Understanding the differences between them is also important for PCB layout , because digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits have different requirements for signal integrity, grounding, power, and noise control. （class B analog audio amplifier） Analog vs Digital Circuits: What Is the Difference? The key difference between analog vs digital circuits is how they represent and process signals. Digital signals focus on discrete states. In a typical digital circuit, voltage is divided into high and low ranges, which are interpreted as 1 and 0. As long as the signal remains within the specified range, small amounts of noise usually do not change the logic result. Analog signals, on the other hand, preserve continuous changes. The small voltage generated by a microphone, the radio-frequency signal received by an antenna, changes in temperature detected by a sensor, and the voltage and current during battery charging and discharging can all vary continuously over time and amplitude. A simple way to understand analog and digital circuits is: A digital signal is like written text. It mainly cares about which character is being represented. An analog signal is like speech. It contains not only information, but also volume, tone, speed, and many subtle changes. In other words, digital circuits are good at processing discrete information, while analog circuits directly interact with continuously changing signals from the real world. （Analog vs Digital Signals） Digital Chips: Computing, Control, and Memory Digital chips are best suited to problems that can be clearly defined and represented as discrete data. Common digital chips include: CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs; MCUs and various controllers; DRAM, SRAM, and NAND Flash; FPGAs; Digital interface and network processing chips. Digital circuits are built from large numbers of logic gates, flip-flops, registers, and memory cells. Driven by a clock, data flows and is processed according to defined rules. Their biggest advantage is their high level of abstraction. Engineers can move from transistors to logic gates, then to adders, processors, instructions, and software. This allows complex systems to be designed, verified, and optimized at different levels of abstraction. Digital chips are particularly suitable for: Executing programs; Storing data; Implementing complex control functions; Performing large-scale logic and mathematical operations; Precisely coordinating different functions within a system. However, digital circuits themselves cannot directly process continuously changing analog signals. A CPU cannot simply take the tiny analog voltage generated by a microphone and process it as digital data. Nor can it directly turn a string of binary data into the continuous analog signal needed to drive a speaker. This is where analog circuits and mixed-signal circuits come in. Analog Chips: Connecting Electronics to the Real World Analog chips process continuously changing voltages and currents. They do not necessarily focus on extremely large amounts of digital logic, but they often determine whether a device can hear clearly, measure accurately, transmit effectively, and charge efficiently. Typical analog and analog-intensive chips include: Operational amplifiers and comparators; Voltage references and analog front ends; Power management chips such as LDOs and DC-DC converters; Audio amplifiers; Analog circuits used in RF front ends. The problems that analog circuits need to solve are very much connected to the real world: How do you amplify a weak signal? How do you filter out unwanted noise? How do you keep an output voltage stable? How do you maintain performance when temperature and supply voltage change? Analog design is challenging because many real-world details cannot simply be abstracted away. Transistor characteristics, temperature, noise, power-supply fluctuations, parasitic resistance, and parasitic capacitance can all affect the final result. Analog circuits, however, often need to pay close attention to the actual signal amplitude, noise, distortion, and offset. It lies in the trade-offs among device characteristics, process technology, noise, temperature, matching, and parasitic effects. Even a seemingly insignificant trace in the layout can introduce additional parasitic effects, noise coupling, or matching problems. And in today's electronic devices, it is rarely one type of chip working alone. Instead, digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits work together as one system. Are More PCB Decoupling Capacitors Always Better? by: Mila Oct 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor PCB decoupling capacitor decoupling capacitor placement PCB power integrity If you have ever designed a PCB schematic , you have probably placed a familiar trio of capacitors near a chip’s power pins: 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF.It seems like a safe bet. Different capacitance values, neatly arranged, ready to keep the power supply stable and suppress noise. But is this tried-and-tested combination always the best choice? When it comes to decoupling capacitors, does adding more always mean better performance? Not necessarily. Effective decoupling depends on more than capacitance alone. Component characteristics, parasitic effects, and PCB layout all play a role. Understanding ESR, ESL, and Self-Resonant Frequenc Circuit theory tells us that the impedance of an ideal capacitor decreases as frequency increases. Real capacitors, however, are not quite so simple. They have two important parasitic parameters: equivalent series resistance (ESR) and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL deserves particular attention. As frequency increases, the capacitive impedance decreases until the capacitor reaches its self-resonant frequency (SRF). Around this frequency, the capacitor typically exhibits its minimum impedance. Beyond SRF, parasitic inductance begins to dominate, and impedance increases with frequency. In other words, a capacitor does not become more effective at filtering noise simply because the frequency keeps rising. Above its SRF, its ability to suppress higher-frequency noise may be limited. That is why selecting a PCB decoupling capacitor requires more than checking its nominal capacitance. You also need to understand how its impedance changes with frequency. How Different Capacitance Values Work Together Capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics. When selected appropriately, they can help maintain low impedance across a wider frequency range in the power distribution network (PDN). 10 µF capacitors are commonly used to provide local charge storage and help reduce impedance over certain low- to mid-frequency ranges. Their actual performance depends on the capacitor type, package, ESR, ESL, and operating voltage. For lower-frequency ripple, the voltage regulator, bulk capacitors, and the overall power network must also be considered. 1 µF capacitors can complement larger and smaller capacitors by helping shape the impedance response over particular frequency ranges. However, whether they effectively fill the gap between other capacitance values depends on the actual impedance curves, not just the nominal capacitance. 0.1 µF capacitors are commonly used for high-frequency decoupling near chip power pins. Although their capacitance is smaller, they can often be placed in compact packages with short connection paths, helping reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Each has its strengths, and combining them can make sense. However, 10 µF, 1 µF, and 0.1 µF are not a universal combination with three fixed frequency ranges. Their effective operating ranges may overlap, and the appropriate values depend on the chip’s requirements, component characteristics, and PCB layout. （capacitor unit conversion chart） How Dielectric and Package Size Affect Decoupling （MLCC Package Size and Decoupling Performance） Two factors that deserve more attention than capacitance alone are dielectric material and package size. Let's start with the dielectric. Suppose you choose a 10 µF ceramic capacitor with a Y5V or Z5U dielectric because it is inexpensive and offers the desired nominal capacitance. Once operating conditions come into play, its capacitance may change significantly with temperature and DC bias voltage. That does not mean these dielectric types are unsuitable for every application. However, their characteristics may make them less suitable for decoupling applications that require stable capacitance. For common power supply decoupling applications, X7R and X5R are often preferred dielectric types. But choosing either one does not guarantee that the nominal capacitance will be available under operating conditions. Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), especially those with high capacitance in small packages, can experience significant capacitance loss under DC bias. Always check the manufacturer's datasheet, particularly the DC bias curve, to determine how much effective capacitance remains at the actual operating voltage. For example, a nominal 10 µF X5R capacitor may provide substantially less capacitance at a particular operating voltage and package size. Even if several capacitors are installed, the effective decoupling capacitance may still be insufficient. Now, let's look at package size. Two 0.1 µF capacitors in 0402 and 0805 packages may have different parasitic characteristics and high-frequency performance. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. However, the actual improvement depends on the component structure, terminal design, and PCB layout. You cannot assume that ESL decreases by a fixed percentage every time the package size is reduced. Sometimes, optimizing the package size and mounting loop can be more effective than simply increasing capacitance. That said, smaller is not always better. Capacitance requirements, voltage rating, soldering reliability, and manufacturing constraints must also be considered. How Parasitics and Anti-Resonance Affect PCB Decoupling Some designers assume that if capacitors with different values can cover different frequency ranges, adding more of them should suppress noise across the board. That sounds reasonable in theory, but reality is more complicated. When multiple capacitors are connected in parallel, their capacitance, ESR, ESL, and PCB interconnect parasitics interact to form a complex impedance network. Under certain conditions, this network can produce an anti-resonance peak, causing the impedance of the power distribution network to rise at a particular frequency. In simple terms, some capacitor branches may behave capacitively while others behave inductively at that frequency. Their interaction, together with interconnect parasitics, can create an impedance peak. The peak's frequency and magnitude depend on the component parameters, connection topology, PCB power planes, and mounting loops. Simply adding or removing capacitors does not guarantee a solution. PCB space is also limited. Adding too many capacitors can crowd routing areas and force some components farther away from the chip's power pins. Longer connection paths can increase loop inductance and weaken high-frequency decoupling performance. So, do not focus only on how many capacitors appear in the schematic. Where they are placed, how they are connected, and how the overall network behaves are equally important. Consider a design example. Suppose a simulation of an FPGA power distribution network reveals a pronounced anti-resonance peak. Adding more capacitors with different capacitance values may not solve the problem and could even make the peak more pronounced. A better approach is to examine the impedance curve, analyze the capacitors' ESR and ESL, evaluate interconnect parasitics, and review the layout. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. PCB Decoupling Capacitor Design: Three Key Principles It comes down to three key principles. 1. Start with the requirements, not guesswork. For high-speed digital circuits, the target impedance method can help guide decoupling design: Here, (Delta V) is the allowable power supply voltage variation, and (Delta I) is the transient current change that the power distribution network must support. First, determine the allowable voltage variation based on the chip's power requirements. Then estimate the target impedance and evaluate the required capacitance values, capacitor count, and placement based on the load's transient behavior and the PDN impedance profile. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Also, proximity alone does not guarantee a good layout. Poor power routing, an indirect ground path, or an unsuitable via connection can still introduce significant parasitic inductance. Remember: High-frequency decoupling is not just about placing a capacitor close to the chip. It is about creating a short, low-inductance current loop. This is one of the most important considerations in decoupling capacitor placement and effective PCB layout. 3. Know when to simplify—but do not remove capacitors blindly. Not every chip needs the full 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. A well-designed network is more reliable than a collection of capacitors added without a clear purpose. （Good vs. Poor Decoupling Capacitor Placement） The 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination is a useful engineering starting point, not a universal rule. There is a sound reason behind it: capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics, and a suitable combination can improve power distribution network performance across different frequency ranges. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. That is the principle behind effective decoupling capacitor selection and PCB power integrity. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Are More PCB Decoupling Capacitors Always Better? by: Mila Oct 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor PCB decoupling capacitor decoupling capacitor placement PCB power integrity If you have ever designed a PCB schematic , you have probably placed a familiar trio of capacitors near a chip’s power pins: 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF.It seems like a safe bet. Different capacitance values, neatly arranged, ready to keep the power supply stable and suppress noise. But is this tried-and-tested combination always the best choice? When it comes to decoupling capacitors, does adding more always mean better performance? Not necessarily. Effective decoupling depends on more than capacitance alone. Component characteristics, parasitic effects, and PCB layout all play a role. Understanding ESR, ESL, and Self-Resonant Frequenc Circuit theory tells us that the impedance of an ideal capacitor decreases as frequency increases. Real capacitors, however, are not quite so simple. They have two important parasitic parameters: equivalent series resistance (ESR) and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL deserves particular attention. As frequency increases, the capacitive impedance decreases until the capacitor reaches its self-resonant frequency (SRF). Around this frequency, the capacitor typically exhibits its minimum impedance. Beyond SRF, parasitic inductance begins to dominate, and impedance increases with frequency. In other words, a capacitor does not become more effective at filtering noise simply because the frequency keeps rising. Above its SRF, its ability to suppress higher-frequency noise may be limited. That is why selecting a PCB decoupling capacitor requires more than checking its nominal capacitance. You also need to understand how its impedance changes with frequency. How Different Capacitance Values Work Together Capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics. When selected appropriately, they can help maintain low impedance across a wider frequency range in the power distribution network (PDN). 10 µF capacitors are commonly used to provide local charge storage and help reduce impedance over certain low- to mid-frequency ranges. Their actual performance depends on the capacitor type, package, ESR, ESL, and operating voltage. For lower-frequency ripple, the voltage regulator, bulk capacitors, and the overall power network must also be considered. 1 µF capacitors can complement larger and smaller capacitors by helping shape the impedance response over particular frequency ranges. However, whether they effectively fill the gap between other capacitance values depends on the actual impedance curves, not just the nominal capacitance. 0.1 µF capacitors are commonly used for high-frequency decoupling near chip power pins. Although their capacitance is smaller, they can often be placed in compact packages with short connection paths, helping reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Each has its strengths, and combining them can make sense. However, 10 µF, 1 µF, and 0.1 µF are not a universal combination with three fixed frequency ranges. Their effective operating ranges may overlap, and the appropriate values depend on the chip’s requirements, component characteristics, and PCB layout. （capacitor unit conversion chart） How Dielectric and Package Size Affect Decoupling （MLCC Package Size and Decoupling Performance） Two factors that deserve more attention than capacitance alone are dielectric material and package size. Let's start with the dielectric. Suppose you choose a 10 µF ceramic capacitor with a Y5V or Z5U dielectric because it is inexpensive and offers the desired nominal capacitance. Once operating conditions come into play, its capacitance may change significantly with temperature and DC bias voltage. That does not mean these dielectric types are unsuitable for every application. However, their characteristics may make them less suitable for decoupling applications that require stable capacitance. For common power supply decoupling applications, X7R and X5R are often preferred dielectric types. But choosing either one does not guarantee that the nominal capacitance will be available under operating conditions. Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), especially those with high capacitance in small packages, can experience significant capacitance loss under DC bias. Always check the manufacturer's datasheet, particularly the DC bias curve, to determine how much effective capacitance remains at the actual operating voltage. For example, a nominal 10 µF X5R capacitor may provide substantially less capacitance at a particular operating voltage and package size. Even if several capacitors are installed, the effective decoupling capacitance may still be insufficient. Now, let's look at package size. Two 0.1 µF capacitors in 0402 and 0805 packages may have different parasitic characteristics and high-frequency performance. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. However, the actual improvement depends on the component structure, terminal design, and PCB layout. You cannot assume that ESL decreases by a fixed percentage every time the package size is reduced. Sometimes, optimizing the package size and mounting loop can be more effective than simply increasing capacitance. That said, smaller is not always better. Capacitance requirements, voltage rating, soldering reliability, and manufacturing constraints must also be considered. How Parasitics and Anti-Resonance Affect PCB Decoupling Some designers assume that if capacitors with different values can cover different frequency ranges, adding more of them should suppress noise across the board. That sounds reasonable in theory, but reality is more complicated. When multiple capacitors are connected in parallel, their capacitance, ESR, ESL, and PCB interconnect parasitics interact to form a complex impedance network. Under certain conditions, this network can produce an anti-resonance peak, causing the impedance of the power distribution network to rise at a particular frequency. In simple terms, some capacitor branches may behave capacitively while others behave inductively at that frequency. Their interaction, together with interconnect parasitics, can create an impedance peak. The peak's frequency and magnitude depend on the component parameters, connection topology, PCB power planes, and mounting loops. Simply adding or removing capacitors does not guarantee a solution. PCB space is also limited. Adding too many capacitors can crowd routing areas and force some components farther away from the chip's power pins. Longer connection paths can increase loop inductance and weaken high-frequency decoupling performance. So, do not focus only on how many capacitors appear in the schematic. Where they are placed, how they are connected, and how the overall network behaves are equally important. Consider a design example. Suppose a simulation of an FPGA power distribution network reveals a pronounced anti-resonance peak. Adding more capacitors with different capacitance values may not solve the problem and could even make the peak more pronounced. A better approach is to examine the impedance curve, analyze the capacitors' ESR and ESL, evaluate interconnect parasitics, and review the layout. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. PCB Decoupling Capacitor Design: Three Key Principles It comes down to three key principles. 1. Start with the requirements, not guesswork. For high-speed digital circuits, the target impedance method can help guide decoupling design: Here, (Delta V) is the allowable power supply voltage variation, and (Delta I) is the transient current change that the power distribution network must support. First, determine the allowable voltage variation based on the chip's power requirements. Then estimate the target impedance and evaluate the required capacitance values, capacitor count, and placement based on the load's transient behavior and the PDN impedance profile. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Also, proximity alone does not guarantee a good layout. Poor power routing, an indirect ground path, or an unsuitable via connection can still introduce significant parasitic inductance. Remember: High-frequency decoupling is not just about placing a capacitor close to the chip. It is about creating a short, low-inductance current loop. This is one of the most important considerations in decoupling capacitor placement and effective PCB layout. 3. Know when to simplify—but do not remove capacitors blindly. Not every chip needs the full 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. A well-designed network is more reliable than a collection of capacitors added without a clear purpose. （Good vs. Poor Decoupling Capacitor Placement） The 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination is a useful engineering starting point, not a universal rule. There is a sound reason behind it: capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics, and a suitable combination can improve power distribution network performance across different frequency ranges. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. That is the principle behind effective decoupling capacitor selection and PCB power integrity. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending by: Mila Oct 15,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout flex PCB design flex PCB bend radius flexible PCB design guidelines Unlike rigid PCBs, flexible PCBs (FPCs) can bend and fold to fit into compact electronic devices. They are widely used in smartphones, laptops, printers, and other products where space is limited or components need to move. However, flexibility does not mean an FPC can bend without limits. Poorly designed bend areas can lead to copper trace cracks, delamination, or premature failure, especially in applications involving repeated bending. A reliable flex PCB design must account for bend radius, trace routing, copper foil selection, and stiffener placement. In this guide, we’ll look at the key design considerations for FPC bend areas and how to improve their reliability in both static and dynamic bending applications. Three Common Flex PCB Bend Area Design Mistakes 1. Keep Vias Out of the Bend Area Vias are one of the key structures to watch when designing a flex PCB bend area. To simplify routing, inexperienced designers may place vias close to a bend line to change layers. However, repeated bending can eventually cause trace fractures and electrical failures. The reason is straightforward: vias introduce structural transitions between the copper plating, pads, and substrate. Differences in material properties and geometry can affect local stress distribution. During repeated bending, stress may concentrate around the via, leading to copper fatigue and crack propagation over time. Eventually, the electrical connection may fail. Design tip: Avoid placing through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias within the active bend area. If layer transitions are necessary, move the vias outside the bend area whenever possible. The required clearance depends on the bend geometry, board thickness, and manufacturer guidelines. A clearance of at least 1 mm can serve as an initial layout reference, but it is not a universal requirement for every FPC. 2. Keep Components Out of the Bend Area Resistors, capacitors, ICs, connectors, and other SMT components should generally not be placed in areas that undergo repeated bending. Components are relatively rigid, while the flexible substrate deforms during bending. If a component sits within the bend area, additional mechanical stress may develop around its body, pads, and solder joints. Brittle components, such as ceramic capacitors, require particular attention because both solder joint cracking and component body damage are possible. Design tip: Place components in rigid sections or reinforced areas, away from the actual bending region. A clearance of 2 mm beyond the bend boundary can serve as an initial reference, but the final distance should account for component size, stiffener geometry, and the actual bending range. 3. Do Not Choose Trace Direction Based on Routing Convenience Alone Trace direction affects how mechanical stress is distributed during bending. However, no single routing angle is best for every FPC structure. When routing through a bend area, consider the actual bending axis, bending direction, and trace distribution. Avoid sharp corners, abrupt width changes, and locally crowded traces, as these features can create stress concentrations. Traces perpendicular to the bending axis: This arrangement may be appropriate for traces crossing the bend area in certain single-axis bending structures, but it must be evaluated against the actual bending geometry. Traces parallel to the bending axis: Whether this arrangement is suitable depends on the specific structure. It should not automatically be classified as the most failure-prone direction. Traces at 45°: Angled routing may work in certain layouts, but its bending life cannot simply be assumed to fall between that of perpendicular and parallel traces. For dynamic flex PCB applications, prioritize smooth, continuous traces, avoid sharp turns and abrupt geometry changes, and verify reliability through appropriate bending tests. (flex PCB bend area design with via and component keepout zones) How to Choose the Right Flex PCB Bend Radius When designing an FPC, some engineers focus mainly on whether it fits inside the enclosure. Reducing the bend radius too much may make assembly easier, but it can also shorten the product's service life. First, distinguish between static and dynamic bending. Their design requirements are different. Static bending: The FPC is bent during assembly and then remains in a relatively fixed position. Internal cables that do not move during normal operation are typical examples. A relatively small bend radius may be acceptable, provided it meets the requirements of the specific material and structure. Dynamic bending: The FPC repeatedly bends during operation. Examples include foldable phone hinges, printer head cables, and robotic joints. These applications place greater demands on copper fatigue resistance, bend radius, and overall structural design. For preliminary flex PCB design, the following values can serve as starting points: Static bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 6 times the total board thickness may be used as an initial reference. Dynamic bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 10 times the total board thickness or greater may be used as an initial reference. These ratios are not universal standards. The actual requirement depends on factors such as single-sided or double-sided construction, copper layer count, copper foil type, material thickness, and the target number of bending cycles. For applications requiring a long flex life, follow the design guidelines provided by the material supplier or FPC manufacturer. For example, if an FPC has a total thickness of 0.2 mm, the preliminary reference values would be: Static bend radius: 0.2 × 6 = 1.2 mm Dynamic bend radius: 0.2 × 10 = 2.0 mm These figures illustrate the calculation method only. They should not be treated as minimum design limits for every 0.2 mm FPC. An excessively small bend radius can cause copper fatigue cracking, coverlay or substrate delamination, and, in severe cases, substrate damage. Any of these failures can eventually render the flexible circuit unusable. RA Copper vs. ED Copper for Flex PCBs Copper foil is an essential part of the FPC's conductive structure and a key factor in repeated-bending reliability. When choosing copper foil, consider whether the application involves static or dynamic bending rather than focusing on cost alone. Electrodeposited copper (ED copper): ED copper is produced through an electrodeposition process and offers mature manufacturing processes and cost advantages. Its grain structure differs from that of rolled copper, and its fatigue performance should be evaluated carefully for repeated-bending applications. For applications involving relatively few bending cycles, ED copper may be considered depending on the specific design and manufacturer recommendations. Rolled-annealed copper (RA copper): RA copper is produced through rolling and annealing. It generally offers good ductility and flexing performance, making it suitable for FPCs that require a longer dynamic flex life. Although it typically costs more, it may help improve reliability in applications involving repeated bending. The key takeaway is simple: For static applications, select copper foil based on cost and performance requirements. For dynamic applications with high cycle counts, RA copper is generally the preferred starting point, subject to verification of the bend radius, copper thickness, and target service life. Flex PCB Routing Guidelines for Reliable Bending In addition to the major design restrictions discussed above, several details deserve attention during flex PCB routing and layout. Trace direction: Determine the routing direction based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces should remain smooth and continuous, with unnecessary sharp turns avoided. Trace width and spacing: Choose appropriate trace widths and spacing to meet electrical and manufacturing requirements. Distribute multiple traces evenly across the bend area instead of crowding them into one section. The final dimensions should account for the bending structure, copper thickness, and manufacturing capabilities rather than relying on a fixed width-to-spacing ratio. Corners and width transitions: Use rounded corners or smooth transitions wherever practical. Avoid sharp corners and abrupt changes in trace width to reduce stress concentrations. Minimize unnecessary crossovers and layer transitions within the bend area. Coverlay: Flexible coverlay is commonly used to protect copper traces in bend areas and reduce the risk of wear and oxidation. Position coverlay openings carefully, keeping coverlay edges away from regions of high mechanical stress. Confirm the required coverage and manufacturing details for the specific design. FPC Stiffeners: Stainless Steel vs. PI Stiffeners increase local rigidity in an FPC. They are commonly used beneath connectors, gold fingers, and SMT components. However, stiffeners should not extend into the active bend area where the FPC needs to flex freely. Stainless steel stiffeners: Stainless steel provides relatively high rigidity and is commonly available in thicknesses of approximately 0.1–0.3 mm. It is often used behind connectors and gold fingers to improve structural support and withstand insertion and removal forces. Pay attention to edge geometry and transitions to prevent sharp edges from damaging the FPC substrate. PI stiffeners: Polyimide (PI) stiffeners are generally thinner and more flexible than metal stiffeners. They can be used beneath certain SMT components or in areas that require localized reinforcement while retaining some flexibility. Their actual rigidity depends on the material thickness and structure. Stress concentrations near stiffener edges should also be considered. Regardless of the stiffener type, keep it outside the active bend area. The required clearance depends on the bending range, stiffener thickness, and overall structure. A fixed 2 mm clearance alone cannot guarantee a reliable design. Static vs. Dynamic Flexing: Key Design Differences Design factorStatic bendingDynamic bendingBend radiusApproximately 6× board thickness as an initial reference; verify the designApproximately 10× board thickness or greater as an initial reference; verify the designCopper foilSelect according to cost and performanceRA copper is generally preferred for high-cycle applicationsLayer countSelect according to electrical and mechanical requirementsMinimize layer count where practical; single- or double-sided designs are often preferredTrace directionDetermine based on the bending geometryDetermine based on the actual motion and bending axisVias and componentsAvoid within the active bend areaAvoid within the active bend areaCoverlayDesign according to structural and protection requirementsPay particular attention to coverlay edges and repeated-bending reliabilityStiffenersPlace outside the active bend areaKeep outside the active bend area and manage edge-related stressTypical applicationsFPCs bent during assembly and then fixed in placeFoldable phones, printer head cables, robotic joints, and other moving assemblies Flex PCB Bend Area Design Checklist Before submitting your FPC design files, use the following checklist to review the bend area: No vias, including through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias, are placed within the bend area. No components or pads unsuitable for bending are placed within the bend area. Trace direction has been evaluated based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces use smooth transitions without sharp corners or abrupt width changes. Multiple traces are distributed evenly to avoid local congestion. The copper foil type matches the static or dynamic bending requirements. The bend radius has been calculated and checked against material and manufacturer requirements. Layer count, copper thickness, and structural design have been evaluated for high-cycle applications. Coverlay openings and edges are positioned away from high-stress regions. Stiffeners remain outside the active bend area, with appropriate edge transitions. A suitable flex-life test plan has been established for critical dynamic applications. Ultimately, successful flex PCB design comes down to controlling bending strain, minimizing local stress concentrations, and ensuring that the materials and structure meet the required flex life. Keep vias and components out of active bend areas, route traces smoothly, allow sufficient bend radius, and select copper foil carefully for dynamic applications. For products that undergo repeated bending, validate the design through testing rather than relying on general rules of thumb alone. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. A clearance of at least 1 mm can serve as an initial layout reference, but it is not a universal requirement for every FPC. 2. Keep Components Out of the Bend Area Resistors, capacitors, ICs, connectors, and other SMT components should generally not be placed in areas that undergo repeated bending. Components are relatively rigid, while the flexible substrate deforms during bending. If a component sits within the bend area, additional mechanical stress may develop around its body, pads, and solder joints. Brittle components, such as ceramic capacitors, require particular attention because both solder joint cracking and component body damage are possible. Design tip: Place components in rigid sections or reinforced areas, away from the actual bending region. A clearance of 2 mm beyond the bend boundary can serve as an initial reference, but the final distance should account for component size, stiffener geometry, and the actual bending range. 3. Do Not Choose Trace Direction Based on Routing Convenience Alone Trace direction affects how mechanical stress is distributed during bending. However, no single routing angle is best for every FPC structure. When routing through a bend area, consider the actual bending axis, bending direction, and trace distribution. Avoid sharp corners, abrupt width changes, and locally crowded traces, as these features can create stress concentrations. Traces perpendicular to the bending axis: This arrangement may be appropriate for traces crossing the bend area in certain single-axis bending structures, but it must be evaluated against the actual bending geometry. Traces parallel to the bending axis: Whether this arrangement is suitable depends on the specific structure. It should not automatically be classified as the most failure-prone direction. Traces at 45°: Angled routing may work in certain layouts, but its bending life cannot simply be assumed to fall between that of perpendicular and parallel traces. For dynamic flex PCB applications, prioritize smooth, continuous traces, avoid sharp turns and abrupt geometry changes, and verify reliability through appropriate bending tests. (flex PCB bend area design with via and component keepout zones) How to Choose the Right Flex PCB Bend Radius When designing an FPC, some engineers focus mainly on whether it fits inside the enclosure. Reducing the bend radius too much may make assembly easier, but it can also shorten the product's service life. First, distinguish between static and dynamic bending. Their design requirements are different. Static bending: The FPC is bent during assembly and then remains in a relatively fixed position. Internal cables that do not move during normal operation are typical examples. A relatively small bend radius may be acceptable, provided it meets the requirements of the specific material and structure. Dynamic bending: The FPC repeatedly bends during operation. Examples include foldable phone hinges, printer head cables, and robotic joints. These applications place greater demands on copper fatigue resistance, bend radius, and overall structural design. For preliminary flex PCB design, the following values can serve as starting points: Static bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 6 times the total board thickness may be used as an initial reference. Dynamic bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 10 times the total board thickness or greater may be used as an initial reference. These ratios are not universal standards. The actual requirement depends on factors such as single-sided or double-sided construction, copper layer count, copper foil type, material thickness, and the target number of bending cycles. For applications requiring a long flex life, follow the design guidelines provided by the material supplier or FPC manufacturer. For example, if an FPC has a total thickness of 0.2 mm, the preliminary reference values would be: Static bend radius: 0.2 × 6 = 1.2 mm Dynamic bend radius: 0.2 × 10 = 2.0 mm These figures illustrate the calculation method only. They should not be treated as minimum design limits for every 0.2 mm FPC. An excessively small bend radius can cause copper fatigue cracking, coverlay or substrate delamination, and, in severe cases, substrate damage. Any of these failures can eventually render the flexible circuit unusable. RA Copper vs. ED Copper for Flex PCBs Copper foil is an essential part of the FPC's conductive structure and a key factor in repeated-bending reliability. When choosing copper foil, consider whether the application involves static or dynamic bending rather than focusing on cost alone. Electrodeposited copper (ED copper): ED copper is produced through an electrodeposition process and offers mature manufacturing processes and cost advantages. Its grain structure differs from that of rolled copper, and its fatigue performance should be evaluated carefully for repeated-bending applications. For applications involving relatively few bending cycles, ED copper may be considered depending on the specific design and manufacturer recommendations. Rolled-annealed copper (RA copper): RA copper is produced through rolling and annealing. It generally offers good ductility and flexing performance, making it suitable for FPCs that require a longer dynamic flex life. Although it typically costs more, it may help improve reliability in applications involving repeated bending. The key takeaway is simple: For static applications, select copper foil based on cost and performance requirements. For dynamic applications with high cycle counts, RA copper is generally the preferred starting point, subject to verification of the bend radius, copper thickness, and target service life. Flex PCB Routing Guidelines for Reliable Bending In addition to the major design restrictions discussed above, several details deserve attention during flex PCB routing and layout. Trace direction: Determine the routing direction based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces should remain smooth and continuous, with unnecessary sharp turns avoided. Trace width and spacing: Choose appropriate trace widths and spacing to meet electrical and manufacturing requirements. Distribute multiple traces evenly across the bend area instead of crowding them into one section. The final dimensions should account for the bending structure, copper thickness, and manufacturing capabilities rather than relying on a fixed width-to-spacing ratio. Corners and width transitions: Use rounded corners or smooth transitions wherever practical. Avoid sharp corners and abrupt changes in trace width to reduce stress concentrations. Minimize unnecessary crossovers and layer transitions within the bend area. Coverlay: Flexible coverlay is commonly used to protect copper traces in bend areas and reduce the risk of wear and oxidation. Position coverlay openings carefully, keeping coverlay edges away from regions of high mechanical stress. Confirm the required coverage and manufacturing details for the specific design. FPC Stiffeners: Stainless Steel vs. PI Stiffeners increase local rigidity in an FPC. They are commonly used beneath connectors, gold fingers, and SMT components. However, stiffeners should not extend into the active bend area where the FPC needs to flex freely. Stainless steel stiffeners: Stainless steel provides relatively high rigidity and is commonly available in thicknesses of approximately 0.1–0.3 mm. It is often used behind connectors and gold fingers to improve structural support and withstand insertion and removal forces. Pay attention to edge geometry and transitions to prevent sharp edges from damaging the FPC substrate. PI stiffeners: Polyimide (PI) stiffeners are generally thinner and more flexible than metal stiffeners. They can be used beneath certain SMT components or in areas that require localized reinforcement while retaining some flexibility. Their actual rigidity depends on the material thickness and structure. Stress concentrations near stiffener edges should also be considered. Regardless of the stiffener type, keep it outside the active bend area. The required clearance depends on the bending range, stiffener thickness, and overall structure. A fixed 2 mm clearance alone cannot guarantee a reliable design. Static vs. Dynamic Flexing: Key Design Differences Design factorStatic bendingDynamic bendingBend radiusApproximately 6× board thickness as an initial reference; verify the designApproximately 10× board thickness or greater as an initial reference; verify the designCopper foilSelect according to cost and performanceRA copper is generally preferred for high-cycle applicationsLayer countSelect according to electrical and mechanical requirementsMinimize layer count where practical; single- or double-sided designs are often preferredTrace directionDetermine based on the bending geometryDetermine based on the actual motion and bending axisVias and componentsAvoid within the active bend areaAvoid within the active bend areaCoverlayDesign according to structural and protection requirementsPay particular attention to coverlay edges and repeated-bending reliabilityStiffenersPlace outside the active bend areaKeep outside the active bend area and manage edge-related stressTypical applicationsFPCs bent during assembly and then fixed in placeFoldable phones, printer head cables, robotic joints, and other moving assemblies Flex PCB Bend Area Design Checklist Before submitting your FPC design files, use the following checklist to review the bend area: No vias, including through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias, are placed within the bend area. No components or pads unsuitable for bending are placed within the bend area. Trace direction has been evaluated based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces use smooth transitions without sharp corners or abrupt width changes. Multiple traces are distributed evenly to avoid local congestion. The copper foil type matches the static or dynamic bending requirements. The bend radius has been calculated and checked against material and manufacturer requirements. Layer count, copper thickness, and structural design have been evaluated for high-cycle applications. Coverlay openings and edges are positioned away from high-stress regions. Stiffeners remain outside the active bend area, with appropriate edge transitions. A suitable flex-life test plan has been established for critical dynamic applications. Ultimately, successful flex PCB design comes down to controlling bending strain, minimizing local stress concentrations, and ensuring that the materials and structure meet the required flex life. Keep vias and components out of active bend areas, route traces smoothly, allow sufficient bend radius, and select copper foil carefully for dynamic applications. For products that undergo repeated bending, validate the design through testing rather than relying on general rules of thumb alone. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
