Verify Now Blog > How to Reduce Crosstalk in PCB Routing: Spacing, 3W Rule, and More How to Reduce Crosstalk in PCB Routing: Spacing, 3W Rule, and More by: Mila Oct 13,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB routing signal integrity，PCB crosstalk，3W rule PCB Many hardware and PCB layout engineers rely heavily on experience when dealing with crosstalk. Routes that are too close may cause interference, while increasing spacing can make routing difficult. Some designers apply the 3W rule to every high-speed signal, while others simply move sensitive traces farther away from potential noise sources. Yet after fabrication, unexpected problems may still appear, including waveform distortion, communication errors, clock instability, and fluctuations in low-level signals. In some cases, PCB crosstalk is part of the problem. Crosstalk is not an unpredictable phenomenon. It can be analyzed, simulated, and controlled through proper PCB routing and layout design. So, how does crosstalk occur? How do trace spacing and parallel routing length affect interference? And why is the widely used 3W rule not a universal solution? Understanding these factors can help you make better routing decisions and improve signal integrity without relying on guesswork. PCB Crosstalk: How Signals Interfere with Each Other Adjacent traces on a PCB can interact through electromagnetic coupling. A trace carrying a high-speed signal, clock signal, or rapidly switching signal is commonly referred to as the aggressor, while a nearby trace affected by the interference is called the victim. Contrary to a common misconception, signals do not simply travel through copper without affecting their surroundings. As a signal propagates along a trace, it creates electric and magnetic fields. When two traces are close together and run parallel for a considerable distance, electromagnetic energy from the aggressor can couple into the victim, introducing unwanted noise voltage or current. This phenomenon is known as PCB crosstalk—essentially, electromagnetic coupling between neighboring signal paths. Several key factors influence the amount of crosstalk: Trace spacing: Under otherwise comparable conditions, smaller spacing generally increases coupling and makes crosstalk more pronounced. Parallel routing length: Longer parallel runs provide more opportunity for electromagnetic coupling. The actual impact depends on propagation delay, signal edge rate, and transmission-line structure. Signal edge rate: Faster rise and fall times generally introduce more high-frequency content, making high-frequency coupling effects more significant. Reference planes and stackup: Continuous reference planes, appropriate dielectric thickness, and suitable layer assignments help control electromagnetic fields and reduce unwanted coupling. These factors explain why slowly changing signals are often easier to manage, while high-speed clocks, DDR interfaces, and other fast signals can become more sensitive to relatively small changes in routing geometry. How Does Trace Spacing Affect Crosstalk? It is tempting to assume that doubling the spacing between traces will halve—or even reduce to one-quarter—the crosstalk. In practice, however, there is no universal mathematical relationship between trace spacing and crosstalk that applies to every PCB design. The coupling between PCB traces depends on several variables, including trace width, spacing, dielectric thickness, reference planes, parallel length, and signal edge rate. Therefore, a simple spacing ratio cannot reliably predict the resulting reduction in crosstalk. In general, increasing the spacing between adjacent traces reduces electromagnetic coupling. This can be particularly effective when the original spacing is very small. However, increasing spacing does not guarantee a fixed percentage reduction in crosstalk. To estimate the actual improvement, designers should evaluate the specific stackup, trace geometry, and signal characteristics through simulation or measurement. In practical PCB routing, spacing rules provide a useful starting point. Signal integrity simulation and crosstalk budgets can then help determine whether the final layout meets the required performance. Capacitive and Inductive Coupling in PCB Routing Crosstalk between PCB traces primarily occurs through electric-field and magnetic-field coupling, commonly described as capacitive coupling and inductive coupling. Both mechanisms may contribute to the overall interference, although their relative importance depends on the routing structure and signal conditions. 1. Capacitive Coupling: Electric-Field Interference Adjacent PCB traces naturally form a parasitic capacitance. When the voltage on the aggressor changes rapidly, current can couple into the victim through this parasitic capacitance. The faster the voltage changes (dv/dt), the more important capacitive coupling may become. In simple terms, faster voltage transitions can increase the impact of capacitive coupling. Clock signals, PWM signals, and fast-switching control signals are common sources of this type of interference. 2. Inductive Coupling: Magnetic-Field Interference Adjacent traces also have mutual inductance. When the current in the aggressor changes rapidly, the surrounding magnetic field changes as well. This changing field can induce an unwanted voltage in the victim. The faster the current changes (di/dt), the more significant inductive coupling may become. In simple terms, rapid current transitions can increase the impact of inductive coupling. Switching power circuits, DC-DC converters, and other circuits with rapidly changing currents deserve particular attention. 3. Differences Between PCB Routing Structures Microstrip: A microstrip trace is routed on an outer PCB layer, with its electromagnetic field distributed through both the surrounding air and the PCB dielectric. Its field distribution differs from that of a stripline, resulting in different coupling characteristics. Stripline: A stripline is routed between two reference planes, which help confine its electromagnetic field within the dielectric. A properly designed stripline structure can improve field containment. In a symmetric structure, capacitive and inductive coupling may also partially cancel at the far end. This is one reason designers may consider routing high-speed signals as striplines when the stackup, impedance requirements, and routing constraints allow it. However, stripline routing does not eliminate crosstalk. Actual performance still depends on the physical structure and design conditions. NEXT vs. FEXT: Near-End and Far-End Crosstalk Crosstalk is commonly classified into two types according to where the interference appears on the victim trace: near-end crosstalk (NEXT) and far-end crosstalk (FEXT). They have different measurement locations and coupling characteristics, so they should be evaluated separately. 1. NEXT: Near-End Crosstalk Near-end crosstalk appears on the victim trace near the aggressor's transmitting end. In typical coupled transmission lines, capacitive and inductive coupling may contribute in the same direction at the near end, resulting in a noticeable noise pulse. The amplitude and duration of NEXT depend on coupling strength, parallel routing length, signal edge rate, and termination conditions. As the coupling length increases, NEXT may eventually approach a saturation level rather than continue increasing indefinitely. In other words, NEXT depends not only on trace spacing but also on coupling length and signal propagation conditions. 2. FEXT: Far-End Crosstalk Far-end crosstalk appears on the victim trace near the receiving end. In some symmetric coupled structures, capacitive and inductive coupling may partially cancel at the far end, potentially making FEXT smaller than NEXT. However, the degree of cancellation depends on the dielectric structure, propagation characteristics, and coupling mode. It should not be assumed to be the same for every PCB design. FEXT may increase with coupling length, but the exact relationship depends on the transmission-line structure and signal conditions. Symmetric, uniform stripline structures can provide favorable far-end crosstalk performance, although actual results still need to be evaluated against the stackup and signal integrity requirements. It is also important to note that NEXT and FEXT do not always appear as fixed wide pulses or narrow spikes. Their actual waveforms depend on the aggressor's edge rate, coupling length, propagation delay, and termination conditions. The 3W Rule in PCB Routing: Benefits and Limitations One common PCB routing guideline is the 3W rule, which recommends a center-to-center spacing of at least three times the trace width between adjacent traces to help reduce electromagnetic coupling. However, meeting the 3W rule does not automatically guarantee acceptable signal integrity. In reality, the 3W rule PCB guideline is an empirical design rule, not a guarantee of a specific crosstalk reduction. It may be sufficient for some ordinary signals, but high-speed interfaces, noise-sensitive circuits, and long parallel routes often require additional evaluation. The following situations deserve particular attention. (3W rule) 1. Between High-Speed Differential Pairs Differential signaling improves immunity to common-mode noise by transmitting signals over a pair of conductors. However, this does not mean that differential pairs are immune to crosstalk from neighboring pairs. Coupling between adjacent differential pairs can affect signal quality, eye diagrams, and bit error rates. Designers should consider differential impedance, pair-to-pair spacing, parallel routing length, and interface requirements rather than applying a universal 5W spacing rule. Where space permits, increasing the spacing between differential pairs and shortening unnecessary parallel runs can help reduce inter-pair crosstalk. 2. Between Clock Signals and Sensitive Signals Clock signals often have fast edge rates and can interfere with nearby sensitive traces. When routing clocks near analog signals, reset lines, or other noise-sensitive nets, prioritize reducing coupling and maintaining a continuous reference plane. Ground shielding may also be considered when appropriate. The required spacing should be determined by the clock edge rate, the victim's noise tolerance, and the PCB stackup. A fixed spacing of 5W–10W or mandatory ground shielding on both sides is not necessary for every clock trace. 3. RF Signals, Analog Signals, and Low-Level Op-Amp Signals These circuits can be particularly sensitive to noise and signal distortion, especially when handling low-amplitude signals or high-impedance nodes. In addition to appropriate trace spacing, designers should consider return paths, grounding, input-to-output isolation, and component placement. For RF traces, grounded vias, shielding, and other isolation techniques may be evaluated according to the specific design. Increasing spacing alone may not solve every problem. Component placement and return-path design are equally important. 4. Long Parallel Buses Long parallel routes provide more opportunity for coupling, particularly when traces are closely spaced and signals have fast edge rates. To reduce crosstalk, minimize unnecessary parallel routing, increase spacing where practical, and consider routing signals on different layers when the stackup permits. When changing layers, ensure that the reference plane remains continuous and that return currents have a suitable path. 5. Dense BGA Fanout Regions BGA fanout regions are often constrained by pad pitch, via dimensions, and the number of available routing layers. Maintaining ideal spacing everywhere may not be practical. Designers can optimize signal assignments, fanout patterns, via placement, and layer transitions to reduce unnecessary parallel routing. For noise-sensitive nets, grounded vias or other grounding structures may help improve isolation when properly designed. In space-constrained regions, prioritize signal integrity on critical nets rather than applying the same spacing requirement indiscriminately to every trace. Ground Guard Traces for Crosstalk Reduction When spacing alone cannot sufficiently reduce coupling, a grounded guard trace between two signal traces may be worth considering. Its effectiveness depends on the grounding method, reference plane, and via arrangement. A less effective approach: Placing a guard trace between two signals without providing a reliable connection to ground. Such a structure may fail to control the electromagnetic field effectively and could introduce additional coupling paths. Better design practices include: Provide reliable grounding: Connect the guard trace to a continuous ground reference to avoid creating an unnecessary floating conductor. Place grounding vias appropriately: Add ground vias along the guard trace, particularly in regions where high-frequency coupling needs to be controlled. Maintain a suitable return path: Ensure low-impedance connections between the grounding structure and the reference plane to avoid disrupting return currents. Determine via spacing based on frequency: Choose via spacing according to the highest relevant frequency, propagation characteristics, and physical structure rather than relying on a universal spacing limit. A grounded guard trace can reduce crosstalk in suitable structures, but the actual improvement depends on frequency, trace geometry, reference planes, and via placement. For demanding designs, simulation or measurement should be used to verify its effectiveness. PCB Crosstalk Reduction Techniques Different crosstalk problems require different solutions. Rather than relying on a single spacing or shielding rule, use the following steps to guide PCB routing decisions. Basic optimization: Increase trace spacing. Increasing the distance between adjacent nets is often a straightforward way to reduce electromagnetic coupling. Advanced optimization: Shorten parallel routing. Minimize unnecessary parallel runs, especially between high-speed signals and noise-sensitive nets. Structural optimization: Maintain continuous reference planes. Provide appropriate return paths and avoid routing across plane splits or other areas that interrupt return currents. Stackup optimization: Choose microstrip or stripline appropriately. Select signal layers according to impedance, routing density, and crosstalk requirements. Where suitable, a symmetric stripline structure can improve electromagnetic field containment. Additional isolation: Consider grounded guard traces. In space-constrained regions or designs with stringent crosstalk requirements, evaluate guard traces, grounding vias, and other shielding techniques. For demanding designs: Verify through simulation and measurement. For high-speed interfaces, sensitive analog networks, and critical clock traces, use crosstalk simulation, eye-diagram analysis, or physical measurements to confirm that the layout meets noise and signal integrity requirements. Conclusion Reducing PCB crosstalk is not simply a matter of increasing trace spacing or applying the 3W rule. The actual results depend on several factors, including coupling mechanisms, parallel routing length, layer structure, reference planes, and signal characteristics. Understanding how these factors interact helps engineers make more informed routing decisions instead of relying on fixed rules alone. Effective PCB routing requires a balance between signal integrity, routing density, and overall board performance. For critical signals, simulation and design verification can help identify potential crosstalk issues before fabrication. By combining sound layout practices with appropriate simulation, engineers can reduce unwanted coupling and build more reliable PCBs. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. When the voltage on the aggressor changes rapidly, current can couple into the victim through this parasitic capacitance. The faster the voltage changes (dv/dt), the more important capacitive coupling may become. In simple terms, faster voltage transitions can increase the impact of capacitive coupling. Clock signals, PWM signals, and fast-switching control signals are common sources of this type of interference. 2. Inductive Coupling: Magnetic-Field Interference Adjacent traces also have mutual inductance. When the current in the aggressor changes rapidly, the surrounding magnetic field changes as well. This changing field can induce an unwanted voltage in the victim. The faster the current changes (di/dt), the more significant inductive coupling may become. In simple terms, rapid current transitions can increase the impact of inductive coupling. Switching power circuits, DC-DC converters, and other circuits with rapidly changing currents deserve particular attention. 3. Differences Between PCB Routing Structures Microstrip: A microstrip trace is routed on an outer PCB layer, with its electromagnetic field distributed through both the surrounding air and the PCB dielectric. Its field distribution differs from that of a stripline, resulting in different coupling characteristics. Stripline: A stripline is routed between two reference planes, which help confine its electromagnetic field within the dielectric. A properly designed stripline structure can improve field containment. In a symmetric structure, capacitive and inductive coupling may also partially cancel at the far end. This is one reason designers may consider routing high-speed signals as striplines when the stackup, impedance requirements, and routing constraints allow it. However, stripline routing does not eliminate crosstalk. Actual performance still depends on the physical structure and design conditions. NEXT vs. FEXT: Near-End and Far-End Crosstalk Crosstalk is commonly classified into two types according to where the interference appears on the victim trace: near-end crosstalk (NEXT) and far-end crosstalk (FEXT). They have different measurement locations and coupling characteristics, so they should be evaluated separately. 1. NEXT: Near-End Crosstalk Near-end crosstalk appears on the victim trace near the aggressor's transmitting end. In typical coupled transmission lines, capacitive and inductive coupling may contribute in the same direction at the near end, resulting in a noticeable noise pulse. The amplitude and duration of NEXT depend on coupling strength, parallel routing length, signal edge rate, and termination conditions. As the coupling length increases, NEXT may eventually approach a saturation level rather than continue increasing indefinitely. In other words, NEXT depends not only on trace spacing but also on coupling length and signal propagation conditions. 2. FEXT: Far-End Crosstalk Far-end crosstalk appears on the victim trace near the receiving end. In some symmetric coupled structures, capacitive and inductive coupling may partially cancel at the far end, potentially making FEXT smaller than NEXT. However, the degree of cancellation depends on the dielectric structure, propagation characteristics, and coupling mode. It should not be assumed to be the same for every PCB design. FEXT may increase with coupling length, but the exact relationship depends on the transmission-line structure and signal conditions. Symmetric, uniform stripline structures can provide favorable far-end crosstalk performance, although actual results still need to be evaluated against the stackup and signal integrity requirements. It is also important to note that NEXT and FEXT do not always appear as fixed wide pulses or narrow spikes. Their actual waveforms depend on the aggressor's edge rate, coupling length, propagation delay, and termination conditions. The 3W Rule in PCB Routing: Benefits and Limitations One common PCB routing guideline is the 3W rule, which recommends a center-to-center spacing of at least three times the trace width between adjacent traces to help reduce electromagnetic coupling. However, meeting the 3W rule does not automatically guarantee acceptable signal integrity. In reality, the 3W rule PCB guideline is an empirical design rule, not a guarantee of a specific crosstalk reduction. It may be sufficient for some ordinary signals, but high-speed interfaces, noise-sensitive circuits, and long parallel routes often require additional evaluation. The following situations deserve particular attention. (3W rule) 1. Between High-Speed Differential Pairs Differential signaling improves immunity to common-mode noise by transmitting signals over a pair of conductors. However, this does not mean that differential pairs are immune to crosstalk from neighboring pairs. Coupling between adjacent differential pairs can affect signal quality, eye diagrams, and bit error rates. Designers should consider differential impedance, pair-to-pair spacing, parallel routing length, and interface requirements rather than applying a universal 5W spacing rule. Where space permits, increasing the spacing between differential pairs and shortening unnecessary parallel runs can help reduce inter-pair crosstalk. 2. Between Clock Signals and Sensitive Signals Clock signals often have fast edge rates and can interfere with nearby sensitive traces. When routing clocks near analog signals, reset lines, or other noise-sensitive nets, prioritize reducing coupling and maintaining a continuous reference plane. Ground shielding may also be considered when appropriate. The required spacing should be determined by the clock edge rate, the victim's noise tolerance, and the PCB stackup. A fixed spacing of 5W–10W or mandatory ground shielding on both sides is not necessary for every clock trace. 3. RF Signals, Analog Signals, and Low-Level Op-Amp Signals These circuits can be particularly sensitive to noise and signal distortion, especially when handling low-amplitude signals or high-impedance nodes. In addition to appropriate trace spacing, designers should consider return paths, grounding, input-to-output isolation, and component placement. For RF traces, grounded vias, shielding, and other isolation techniques may be evaluated according to the specific design. Increasing spacing alone may not solve every problem. Component placement and return-path design are equally important. 4. Long Parallel Buses Long parallel routes provide more opportunity for coupling, particularly when traces are closely spaced and signals have fast edge rates. To reduce crosstalk, minimize unnecessary parallel routing, increase spacing where practical, and consider routing signals on different layers when the stackup permits. When changing layers, ensure that the reference plane remains continuous and that return currents have a suitable path. 5. Dense BGA Fanout Regions BGA fanout regions are often constrained by pad pitch, via dimensions, and the number of available routing layers. Maintaining ideal spacing everywhere may not be practical. Designers can optimize signal assignments, fanout patterns, via placement, and layer transitions to reduce unnecessary parallel routing. For noise-sensitive nets, grounded vias or other grounding structures may help improve isolation when properly designed. In space-constrained regions, prioritize signal integrity on critical nets rather than applying the same spacing requirement indiscriminately to every trace. Ground Guard Traces for Crosstalk Reduction When spacing alone cannot sufficiently reduce coupling, a grounded guard trace between two signal traces may be worth considering. Its effectiveness depends on the grounding method, reference plane, and via arrangement. A less effective approach: Placing a guard trace between two signals without providing a reliable connection to ground. Such a structure may fail to control the electromagnetic field effectively and could introduce additional coupling paths. Better design practices include: Provide reliable grounding: Connect the guard trace to a continuous ground reference to avoid creating an unnecessary floating conductor. Place grounding vias appropriately: Add ground vias along the guard trace, particularly in regions where high-frequency coupling needs to be controlled. Maintain a suitable return path: Ensure low-impedance connections between the grounding structure and the reference plane to avoid disrupting return currents. Determine via spacing based on frequency: Choose via spacing according to the highest relevant frequency, propagation characteristics, and physical structure rather than relying on a universal spacing limit. A grounded guard trace can reduce crosstalk in suitable structures, but the actual improvement depends on frequency, trace geometry, reference planes, and via placement. For demanding designs, simulation or measurement should be used to verify its effectiveness. PCB Crosstalk Reduction Techniques Different crosstalk problems require different solutions. Rather than relying on a single spacing or shielding rule, use the following steps to guide PCB routing decisions. Basic optimization: Increase trace spacing. Increasing the distance between adjacent nets is often a straightforward way to reduce electromagnetic coupling. Advanced optimization: Shorten parallel routing. Minimize unnecessary parallel runs, especially between high-speed signals and noise-sensitive nets. Structural optimization: Maintain continuous reference planes. Provide appropriate return paths and avoid routing across plane splits or other areas that interrupt return currents. Stackup optimization: Choose microstrip or stripline appropriately. Select signal layers according to impedance, routing density, and crosstalk requirements. Where suitable, a symmetric stripline structure can improve electromagnetic field containment. Additional isolation: Consider grounded guard traces. In space-constrained regions or designs with stringent crosstalk requirements, evaluate guard traces, grounding vias, and other shielding techniques. For demanding designs: Verify through simulation and measurement. For high-speed interfaces, sensitive analog networks, and critical clock traces, use crosstalk simulation, eye-diagram analysis, or physical measurements to confirm that the layout meets noise and signal integrity requirements. Conclusion Reducing PCB crosstalk is not simply a matter of increasing trace spacing or applying the 3W rule. The actual results depend on several factors, including coupling mechanisms, parallel routing length, layer structure, reference planes, and signal characteristics. Understanding how these factors interact helps engineers make more informed routing decisions instead of relying on fixed rules alone. Effective PCB routing requires a balance between signal integrity, routing density, and overall board performance. For critical signals, simulation and design verification can help identify potential crosstalk issues before fabrication. By combining sound layout practices with appropriate simulation, engineers can reduce unwanted coupling and build more reliable PCBs. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Design and Layout Guidelines for LDO and DCDC Power Supply Design and Layout Guidelines for LDO and DCDC by: Mila Sep 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design DCDC PCB layout power supply layout LDO layout guidelines Power supply design is not simply about choosing the right regulator and adding enough copper. The PCB layout directly affects thermal performance, noise, EMI, stability, and overall power integrity. LDOs and DCDC converters have different layout priorities: LDOs require careful attention to heat dissipation, capacitor placement, and power loss, while DCDC converters are more sensitive to high-frequency current loops, feedback routing, and grounding. When both are used in the same system, power-stage isolation and decoupling become equally important. In this guide, we’ll break down the key power supply layout considerations and common mistakes for LDOs, DCDC converters, and mixed power architectures. 1. LDO (Low-Dropout Regulator): Quiet but Sensitive to Heat （LDO regulator） Advantages: Low noise, no switching interference, and simple peripheral circuitry Disadvantages: Efficiency depends on the input-to-output voltage difference, and large voltage drops or high load currents can generate significant heat. Three Common LDO PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Poor Thermal Management → Excessive Temperature Rise Incorrect: Leaving the exposed pad floating without sufficient copper area or thermal vias. Consequence: Higher thermal resistance can increase junction temperature, potentially triggering thermal protection or affecting long-term reliability. Correct: Connect the exposed pad to a sufficiently large copper area. Add thermal vias according to the package and datasheet recommendations, connecting them to internal or bottom-layer copper planes. Avoid routing signal traces underneath the thermal pad. Evaluate the required copper area and thermal performance based on actual power dissipation. Mistake 2: Input/Output Capacitors Too Far from the Pins → Reduced Stability and Transient Performance Incorrect: Placing the input and output capacitors far away from the LDO pins. Consequence: Increased parasitic impedance can affect stability, transient response, and high-frequency noise performance. Correct: Place Cin and Cout as close as possible to the corresponding LDO pins. Select capacitor values, quantities, and ESR according to the device datasheet. Prefer low-ESR capacitors recommended by the manufacturer. Keep the feedback path short and avoid unnecessary routing and noise coupling. Mistake 3: Ignoring Voltage Drop and Power Dissipation → Efficiency and Thermal Issues Incorrect: Using an LDO for high input voltage and high current without evaluating power dissipation. Consequence: Higher LDO power dissipation increases junction temperature and may trigger thermal protection or reduce system reliability. Correct: The main power dissipation of an LDO can be estimated using: P ≈ (Vin − Vout) × Iout The larger the voltage drop and output current, the higher the LDO power dissipation. For high-power applications, evaluate efficiency, junction temperature, and PCB thermal performance together. When the voltage drop or load current is high, consider using a DCDC converter first and an LDO for downstream regulation and noise reduction. 2. DCDC (Switching Power Supply): Efficient but Noisy （dc-dc converter） Advantages: High conversion efficiency, higher output current capability, and suitability for a wide range of input and output voltages Disadvantages: Switching nodes and high di/dt currents can generate noise, making DCDC PCB layout critical to EMI, stability, and overall power performance. Five Common DCDC PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Long Power Loops → Increased Ringing and EMI Incorrect: Placing the input capacitor, power switch, inductor, and other key components too far apart, resulting in a large high-frequency current loop. Consequence: Increased parasitic inductance can produce more pronounced voltage spikes and ringing under high di/dt conditions, increasing EMI and component stress. Correct: Minimize the area of critical high-frequency power loops. Place input bypass capacitors, power devices, and inductors as close together as possible. Use sufficiently wide power traces. The required width should be determined by current, copper thickness, and allowable temperature rise. Avoid unnecessarily long high di/dt return paths. Mistake 2: Noisy Feedback Path → Output Voltage Fluctuation Incorrect: Routing the FB trace close to or parallel with the SW node, inductor, or other noisy areas. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into the feedback network, affecting output voltage regulation and system stability. Correct: Keep the FB trace short and away from the SW node and high di/dt current paths. Place the feedback resistors close to the IC's FB pin. Sense the output voltage from a stable, low-noise point. For high-precision applications, consider Kelvin sensing or other methods recommended by the device manufacturer to reduce voltage drop and noise. Mistake 3: Improper Ground Plane Design → Increased EMI and Noise Incorrect: Improper AGND, PGND, or high-current return-path routing causes sensitive control circuitry to share impedance with power return currents. Consequence: Ground bounce and common-impedance coupling can affect control signals, feedback, and output voltage. Correct: Follow the DCDC IC manufacturer's recommended method for connecting AGND and PGND. Provide a low-impedance return path for PGND. Keep sensitive analog ground areas away from high-current power return paths whenever possible. Prevent high di/dt currents from passing through sensitive signal areas. Mistake 4: Improper Input Capacitor Placement → Increased Input Ripple Incorrect: Relying on a single bulk capacitor while placing it far from the VIN and GND pins. Consequence: A larger high-frequency current loop can increase input ripple and noise. Correct: Configure input capacitors according to the DCDC converter datasheet. Use capacitors with different values when necessary to address different frequency ranges. Place input capacitors as close as possible to the VIN and GND pins. Keep the input capacitor loop short and compact. Mistake 5: Ignoring the Freewheeling Path → Reduced Efficiency and Poorer EMI Performance Incorrect: Placing the freewheeling diode, synchronous MOSFET, or related circuitry too far apart. Consequence: Increased parasitic parameters can lead to additional losses, ringing, and EMI. Correct: Optimize the freewheeling and synchronous rectification paths according to the specific converter topology. Minimize high-current return paths. For multiphase DCDC converters, keep the power paths of each phase well organized and reasonably symmetrical. 3. LDO + DCDC Mixed Power Supply: Balancing Efficiency and Low Noise （power supply pcb） In practical systems, DCDC converters and LDOs are often used together rather than as alternatives. For example: DCDC: 12V → 3.3V for efficient voltage conversion LDO: 3.3V → 1.8V for noise-sensitive circuits such as ADCs, PLLs, and clocks This approach combines the efficiency of a DCDC converter with the low-noise characteristics of an LDO, making it useful for applications that require both power efficiency and clean power rails. Three Common Mixed Power Supply Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Insufficient Filtering at the LDO Input → Upstream Noise May Reach the Downstream Rail Incorrect: Connecting the DCDC output directly to an LDO-powered sensitive load without evaluating the DCDC switching noise and the LDO's PSRR. Consequence: Switching ripple from the upstream converter may couple into downstream sensitive circuits through the power path, affecting ADC, PLL, and other noise-sensitive devices. Correct: Evaluate whether additional filtering is required based on the DCDC switching frequency, LDO PSRR, and load noise requirements. When necessary, add a ferrite bead, LC filter, or π filter between the two power stages. Place filtering components close to the corresponding power input and keep the filter loop area under control. Avoid adding filtering components blindly; select them based on the actual noise frequency range. Mistake 2: Poor Power Region Layout → Noise Coupling Incorrect: Placing the high-noise DCDC switching area too close to sensitive LDO power areas or creating unnecessary coupling between different power regions. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into sensitive power rails through parasitic capacitance, electromagnetic coupling, or shared impedance. Correct: Properly separate the DCDC power stage, LDO area, and sensitive load areas. Keep high-noise SW nodes away from sensitive power rails and signals. Maintain a solid reference ground plane beneath the LDO output power area whenever possible. Keep sensitive power traces away from high di/dt return paths of the DCDC converter. Mistake 3: Poorly Designed Decoupling Network → Insufficient High-Frequency Response Incorrect: Placing all capacitors at the DCDC output while providing insufficient local decoupling near sensitive loads. Consequence: Parasitic impedance in the power path can reduce high-frequency decoupling effectiveness, preventing the load from receiving transient current quickly enough. Correct: Configure DCDC output capacitors according to the converter requirements. Use the required input and output capacitors at the LDO according to the datasheet. Add local decoupling capacitors close to sensitive loads such as ADCs, PLLs, and MCUs. Design each power stage's decoupling network according to the actual load and frequency requirements rather than simply adding more capacitors. Conclusion Although LDOs and DCDC converters are both power management devices, their power supply layout priorities are different. LDO layout guidelines focus more on thermal management, capacitor placement, and power dissipation. DCDC PCB layout focuses more on high-frequency power loops, feedback paths, grounding, and EMI. Mixed power supplies require additional attention to noise isolation and decoupling between different power stages. A good power supply pcb design is not simply about adding more copper. It is about giving current the shortest and most appropriate path, keeping noise away from sensitive areas, and placing every critical component where it can perform properly. Verify Now Blog > Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips by: Mila Oct 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Reflow Soldering Wave Soldering SMT vs. THT PCB Assembly PCB Soldering As hardware engineers, we design the PCB, select the components, and send the Gerber files to the manufacturer. But have you ever wondered why some components go through reflow soldering while others require wave soldering? Both processes melt solder to form electrical and mechanical connections, so why does a production line need two different types of equipment? The reason is not that equipment manufacturers are making the process unnecessarily complicated. The main difference between reflow soldering and wave soldering lies in how the solder reaches the joints and which types of components each process is best suited for. For hardware engineers, understanding these two processes is more than just useful knowledge. It can affect PCB layout , component selection, pad design, and even troubleshooting during manufacturing. How Reflow Soldering Works Reflow soldering is primarily used for surface-mount technology (SMT) components, such as resistors, capacitors, SOPs, QFNs, and BGAs. The basic process is straightforward: solder paste is first printed onto the PCB pads, and the components are then placed on the board. Next, the PCB assembly passes through a reflow oven, where the solder paste goes through several stages, including preheating, heating, time above the liquidus temperature, and cooling. These stages allow the solder to melt, wet the surfaces, and solidify to form reliable joints. One detail that is easy to overlook is that reflow soldering is not simply about heating the entire PCB to a fixed temperature. The temperature profile over time must be carefully controlled. Taking the common SAC305 lead-free solder alloy as an example, its melting range is approximately 217–220°C. During reflow, the solder joint temperature must rise above the liquidus temperature and remain there for a certain period. However, the peak temperature, time above liquidus, and heating and cooling rates depend on factors such as the solder paste, component temperature limits, and PCB thermal mass. These parameters cannot be applied universally to every board. （reflow soldering） How Wave Soldering Works Imagine a PCB with small resistors, large connectors, and power pads connected to extensive copper areas. Small components generally have lower thermal mass and heat up quickly, while large components and pads absorb more heat and may heat up more slowly. If the temperature rises too quickly, the small components may approach their peak temperature before the solder on the larger pads has fully melted. On the other hand, increasing the peak temperature too much or extending the time at high temperatures to accommodate the larger pads can increase thermal stress on components, damage the PCB, and raise the risk of solder oxidation. The real challenge of reflow soldering is to ensure that every solder joint receives enough heat, but not excessive heat, while staying within the temperature limits of the components. （wave soldering） Why Reflow Temperature Control Matters Wave soldering works in a more straightforward way. The equipment melts the solder and uses a pump to create a stable wave of molten solder. After the PCB passes through flux application and preheating, its solder side comes into contact with the molten solder. The solder wets the component leads and PCB pads, forming the joints. Traditional wave soldering is most commonly used for through-hole technology (THT) components, such as through-hole connectors, transformers, relay sockets, and some power components. Their leads pass through holes in the PCB, allowing the molten solder to contact the leads and pads from the solder side and form reliable joints. Why Wave Soldering Isn't Suitable for Every PCB Wave soldering brings molten solder into direct contact with the solder side of the PCB. If the board contains a large number of surface-mount components, especially fine-pitch leads or packages with bottom-side pads, solder may bridge adjacent leads or cause soldering defects in components that are unsuitable for this process. However, this does not mean that surface-mount components can never be wave soldered. When wave soldering is used for suitable SMT components, the component orientation, pad spacing, and solder mask design must be considered carefully. In some cases, adhesive is also used to hold the components in place during soldering. PCB travel direction, protruding lead length, and component placement on the solder side must also be taken into account. If the design is unsuitable, even well-adjusted equipment parameters may not be enough to ensure consistent production quality. It is worth noting that reflow soldering is not limited to surface-mount components, nor is wave soldering restricted to through-hole components. Other processes, including selective wave soldering and pin-in-paste soldering (also known as intrusive reflow soldering), are used in actual manufacturing. The appropriate method depends on package structures, component distribution, solder joint reliability, and production requirements. （PCB Assembly） PCB Design Considerations for Reflow and Wave Soldering 1. Component and Pad Design For SMT packages such as QFNs and BGAs, engineers need to consider pad dimensions, solder paste printing, stencil design, and the reflow temperature profile. For through-hole components, important factors include hole diameter, copper thickness, lead dimensions, and solder fill. Package and pad design affect not only electrical performance but also soldering quality during PCB assembly. 2. Copper Distribution and Thermal Management When a power component's pad is connected to a large copper area, the copper can absorb and distribute heat, making it more difficult for the local pad to reach the required temperature. This may prevent the solder from melting sufficiently. During design, engineers should evaluate copper distribution, pad structure, and the actual temperature profile rather than simply increasing the oven temperature to compensate. 3. Common Soldering Defects and Their Causes For example, tombstoning of resistors after reflow soldering may result from uneven heating between the two pads, differences in solder paste volume, or component placement errors. Solder bridging between connector leads after wave soldering may be related to pad spacing, lead orientation, flux application, or wave parameters. When these defects occur, engineers should investigate the PCB design and soldering process alongside the components themselves. Hardware engineers do not necessarily need to operate soldering equipment themselves, but they should understand how their designs affect manufacturability. Reflow soldering focuses on controlling the temperature profile during solder paste melting, while wave soldering focuses on controlling the contact between molten solder and the PCB's solder side. Neither process is universally better than the other. The right choice depends on component packages, PCB layout, and production requirements. Why Do PCBs Need Stitching Vias Along the Board Edge? by: Mila Oct 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout stitching vias PCB EMI shielding PCB return path PCB via stitching Anyone who has worked on PCB layout has probably experienced this: after finishing the layout, you hand the board over to a senior engineer for review. They take a quick look around the board and ask, “Where are the ground vias along the edge?” At first, this may seem unnecessary. After all, the board edge does not carry signal traces. So why are stitching vias placed there? The answer lies in what happens around the edge of a PCB. Properly placed grounding vias can help control electromagnetic coupling, provide a more continuous high-frequency return path, and improve PCB edge shielding. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive designs, that simple row of vias can make a noticeable difference. （Stitching Vias） What Do Ground Vias Along the PCB Edge Actually Do? This row of vias is commonly known as a ground via fence, via fence, or stitching vias. It is not simply a matter of placing a row of vias around the board. Instead, the vias connect ground structures on different PCB layers and create a more continuous electromagnetic boundary along the board edge. For high-speed, RF, and high-reliability PCBs, the main benefits include improving high-frequency return paths, reducing electromagnetic leakage and coupling, and enhancing the continuity of local shielding structures. 1. Reduce Electromagnetic Leakage and Improve EMI Performance The PCB edge is the boundary between copper, dielectric material, and air. When high-speed, clock, or RF signals pass through the board, relatively strong electromagnetic fields may exist around this region. If the reference ground structure around the PCB edge is discontinuous, electromagnetic fields can couple outward through the edge, increasing EMI risks. External interference can also couple into sensitive circuits through the same region. A continuous row of grounding vias creates a low-impedance grounding boundary around the PCB edge. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? Many engineers think of the grounding vias around a PCB edge as a small Faraday cage. There is some truth to this analogy, but an important point should be noted: a PCB via fence is not an ideal, completely enclosed Faraday cage. The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. Therefore, instead of simply applying a fixed wavelength ratio, the via spacing should be determined based on the actual operating frequency, signal rise time, and PCB structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. Limitations A PCB via fence cannot completely prevent electromagnetic coupling at all frequencies. Copper and grounding vias alone have limited effectiveness against low-frequency magnetic fields. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. How Should You Design Stitching Vias Along the PCB Edge? Adding vias around the board is not simply a matter of placing them in a row. Via spacing, location, grounding method, and edge copper design all need to be considered according to the actual PCB structure. Here are some common design principles. 1. Via Spacing A common engineering approach is to estimate the via spacing based on the wavelength corresponding to the target frequency. For example, λ/10 or a smaller spacing can be used as an initial reference. However, this is not a fixed standard that applies to every PCB. Actual design should also consider: The highest frequency of interest High-speed signal rise/fall time PCB stackup Reference plane location Board-edge structure Shielding-can and connector openings For ordinary PCBs, relatively wider via spacing may be sufficient. For high-speed, RF, or high-EMI areas, the spacing may need to be reduced. Common engineering reference values include: General PCBs: approximately 50–100 mil High-speed/RF areas: approximately 30–50 mil Areas with stringent shielding requirements: further spacing reduction based on simulation or actual EMI testing Do not mechanically apply a fixed value. The final via spacing should be determined based on the actual frequency and structure. 2. Via Location Edge grounding vias should maintain an appropriate clearance from the PCB outline. Sufficient clearance should be provided according to the PCB manufacturer's fabrication capability to prevent damage to the vias during routing, milling, V-cut, or other board-edge processing. At the same time: Distribute the vias evenly along the board edge whenever possible. Avoid large gaps in the via fence. Increase via density around RF, high-speed signal, and connector areas when necessary. Connect the grounding vias to the appropriate reference ground plane rather than only to the top-layer copper. It is important to note that not every ground plane needs to be connected through the same via. The exact connection method should be determined based on the PCB stackup and return-current path. 3. Start With Continuous Ground Copper Many designers add a row of vias but overlook the ground copper between them. This alone cannot create a complete PCB ground via fence. A continuous ground copper area should be provided around the PCB edge according to the board structure, with grounding vias connecting it to the internal reference ground plane. The vias provide vertical connections, while continuous ground copper provides horizontal connections. Together, they form a more complete grounding boundary. High-speed signal traces, slots, or other structures should not arbitrarily cut through this grounding boundary. 4. Increase Via Density in Critical Areas The entire PCB does not necessarily need the same via spacing. The following areas may require additional stitching vias: Board-edge connectors and interfaces: Connectors are important paths through which external signals enter the PCB. Proper grounding vias can improve the return path around the interface and reduce edge coupling. Shielding-can areas: Dense grounding vias around the shielding-can solder pad can create a more continuous high-frequency grounding path. RF and high-speed clock areas: For areas that are particularly sensitive to EMI or crosstalk, reducing the via spacing can strengthen local shielding. Conclusion Proper stitching vias are an important part of high-speed PCB layout and PCB design .Their core function is to improve high-frequency return paths around the PCB edge and reduce electromagnetic coupling and EMI leakage through the combination of stitching vias and continuous reference-ground structures. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive PCBs, proper PCB via stitching and PCB edge shielding are particularly important. But remember: more vias are not always better, and not every PCB needs a dense row of grounding vias. Via spacing, edge clearance, reference planes, and local shielding structures should all be determined based on the actual signal frequency, rise time, and PCB stackup. For high-speed, RF, and high-reliability PCBs, the main benefits include improving high-frequency return paths, reducing electromagnetic leakage and coupling, and enhancing the continuity of local shielding structures. 1. Reduce Electromagnetic Leakage and Improve EMI Performance The PCB edge is the boundary between copper, dielectric material, and air. When high-speed, clock, or RF signals pass through the board, relatively strong electromagnetic fields may exist around this region. If the reference ground structure around the PCB edge is discontinuous, electromagnetic fields can couple outward through the edge, increasing EMI risks. External interference can also couple into sensitive circuits through the same region. A continuous row of grounding vias creates a low-impedance grounding boundary around the PCB edge. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? Many engineers think of the grounding vias around a PCB edge as a small Faraday cage. There is some truth to this analogy, but an important point should be noted: a PCB via fence is not an ideal, completely enclosed Faraday cage. The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. Therefore, instead of simply applying a fixed wavelength ratio, the via spacing should be determined based on the actual operating frequency, signal rise time, and PCB structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. Limitations A PCB via fence cannot completely prevent electromagnetic coupling at all frequencies. Copper and grounding vias alone have limited effectiveness against low-frequency magnetic fields. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. How Should You Design Stitching Vias Along the PCB Edge? Adding vias around the board is not simply a matter of placing them in a row. Via spacing, location, grounding method, and edge copper design all need to be considered according to the actual PCB structure. Here are some common design principles. 1. Via Spacing A common engineering approach is to estimate the via spacing based on the wavelength corresponding to the target frequency. For example, λ/10 or a smaller spacing can be used as an initial reference. However, this is not a fixed standard that applies to every PCB. Actual design should also consider: The highest frequency of interest High-speed signal rise/fall time PCB stackup Reference plane location Board-edge structure Shielding-can and connector openings For ordinary PCBs, relatively wider via spacing may be sufficient. For high-speed, RF, or high-EMI areas, the spacing may need to be reduced. Common engineering reference values include: General PCBs: approximately 50–100 mil High-speed/RF areas: approximately 30–50 mil Areas with stringent shielding requirements: further spacing reduction based on simulation or actual EMI testing Do not mechanically apply a fixed value. The final via spacing should be determined based on the actual frequency and structure. 2. Via Location Edge grounding vias should maintain an appropriate clearance from the PCB outline. Sufficient clearance should be provided according to the PCB manufacturer's fabrication capability to prevent damage to the vias during routing, milling, V-cut, or other board-edge processing. At the same time: Distribute the vias evenly along the board edge whenever possible. Avoid large gaps in the via fence. Increase via density around RF, high-speed signal, and connector areas when necessary. Connect the grounding vias to the appropriate reference ground plane rather than only to the top-layer copper. It is important to note that not every ground plane needs to be connected through the same via. The exact connection method should be determined based on the PCB stackup and return-current path. 3. Start With Continuous Ground Copper Many designers add a row of vias but overlook the ground copper between them. This alone cannot create a complete PCB ground via fence. A continuous ground copper area should be provided around the PCB edge according to the board structure, with grounding vias connecting it to the internal reference ground plane. The vias provide vertical connections, while continuous ground copper provides horizontal connections. Together, they form a more complete grounding boundary. High-speed signal traces, slots, or other structures should not arbitrarily cut through this grounding boundary. 4. Increase Via Density in Critical Areas The entire PCB does not necessarily need the same via spacing. The following areas may require additional stitching vias: Board-edge connectors and interfaces: Connectors are important paths through which external signals enter the PCB. Proper grounding vias can improve the return path around the interface and reduce edge coupling. Shielding-can areas: Dense grounding vias around the shielding-can solder pad can create a more continuous high-frequency grounding path. RF and high-speed clock areas: For areas that are particularly sensitive to EMI or crosstalk, reducing the via spacing can strengthen local shielding. Conclusion Proper stitching vias are an important part of high-speed PCB layout and PCB design .Their core function is to improve high-frequency return paths around the PCB edge and reduce electromagnetic coupling and EMI leakage through the combination of stitching vias and continuous reference-ground structures. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive PCBs, proper PCB via stitching and PCB edge shielding are particularly important. But remember: more vias are not always better, and not every PCB needs a dense row of grounding vias. Via spacing, edge clearance, reference planes, and local shielding structures should all be determined based on the actual signal frequency, rise time, and PCB stackup. RP2350-USB-C Microcontroller Development Board Based Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips Meet PCBWay at EPTECH 2026 in Calgary, Canada Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity.
